speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes at my disposal yesterday evening I tried to make the point that we are having tremendous difficulty in amending our constitution partly because of the fundamentally different approach to the matter adopted by this government under the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the provinces, and this remark applies to all provinces
January 27, 1970

regardless of the political party that forms the provincial government. There is an impression abroad that the Prime Minister is interested in changing the constitution only so far as that change will spell out the rights of French speaking people of Canada and give them an equal opportunity to use their language in all parts of Canada. It seems to some that that is the only aspect in which this government is interested. The provinces are tremendously interested in a whole range of priorities and in financing programs for which, under the provisions of the BNA Act, they are responsible.
The hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher) who spoke last night suggested that in amending the constitution we might consider limiting the taxing powers of the government and the amount of money it can spend. In his introductory remarks yesterday the Prime Minister pointed out that between 1954 and 1964 the expenditures of the federal government had increased only by about 56 per cent, while the expenditures of provincial governments increased by some 204 per cent. The expenditures of my province, Manitoba, between the years 1958 and 1968 rose, under a Conservative government, from about $80 million annually to over $350 million annually, an increase of about 400 per cent. I am not criticizing the former Conservative government headed by former Premier Roblin for being a spending government. The money had to be spent simply because the Conservative government of Manitoba realized that it was necessary to bring Manitoba into the twentieth century in such fields as education, health and welfare, the building of roads and other important fields under provincial jurisdiction.
Not many years ago most young people in this country, and particularly those living in rural areas, did not attend high school. Today, the program under which young people may attend high school extends to almost all parts Of Canada. Indeed, there has been a fantastic increase in the percentage of our young people attending universities. In this field the provinces must play an important role and face tremendous expenditures. I am certain that most provinces would be more than happy if the federal government were prepared to take over either the responsibility of financing university education or make available sources of taxation which the provinces could use to finance education. As yet, however, there is no indication that the federal government is interested in even discussing this matter with the provinces.
Canadian Constitution
We have seen an astronomical increase in provincial expenditures and responsibilities in the fields of health and welfare. Every province of Canada now has a provincial hospitalization program under which hospital expenses are paid by the province and not the individual who must go to hospital. Similarly, in the very near future every province in Canada will be participating in the medicare plan proposed by the federal government and financed jointly by the federal government and the provinces. All this has meant, and will mean, a tremendous increase in provincial spending. The provinces will need more money and they cannot help but be disturbed by the almost casual announcement the Prime Minister made, an announcement that was echoed by some of his ministers, that the federal government is thinking of getting out of programs in which it persuaded provinces to participate. There are similar problems of urban blight, urban renewal and the provision of housing for people in the low income brackets, people on welfare and, indeed people in middle income brackets who are finding that their incomes today are not sufficient to enable them to purchase a house using the normal methods of financing.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
A few moments ago, in answer to a question put by my colleague the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) in charge of housing reported that last year the federal government had financed the building of approximately 29,000 public housing units. That, Mr. Speaker, is just over 10 per cent of the total number of houses built last year. Only 10 per cent of the houses built last year were for the people who needed them most. People earning $6,000 or $7,000 a year cannot purchase a house and must rent accommodation. These are the people who require public housing, yet the minister has announced that just over 10 per cent of the houses built last year were of this type.
I suggest the people who are in the income bracket between $12,000 and $20,000, and sometimes in excess of that, can wait for housing. They already have adequate housing. The people to whom I am referring are earning under $6,000 a year and are living in the central cores of the cities in dilapidated housing. These people require more than 10 per cent of the total housing being built in this country. How will this requirement be met when the federal government under the present Prime Minister, believes that the prob-

January 27, 1970
Canadian Constitution
lems of the cities are a provincial responsibility, that the federal government should not take a leading role in such problems as building homes and rapid transit systems so that people can move to the centre of the city where they work. How can we get the federal government to accept this responsibility? Because the provinces do not receive the required leadership from the federal government, they are not too concerned about constitutional conferences to be held in the future. They are not interested because the federal government is not dealing with the problems which are of primary concern to them.
One problem which has come to the fore and is being discussed in the press, on television is pollution. The problem of pollution is one in which the jurisdiction is divided between the federal, provincial and municipal governments. During the question period today, the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Simpson) directed a question to the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) about the pollution problem in Manitoba. Fish in Manitoba lakes have been found to contain mercury poisoning. This mercury was dumped into the rivers in Saskatchewan, carried into lakes in Manitoba and is now poisoning the fish in Lake Manitoba. This is an interprovincial problem which requires participation by the federal government. Even though a couple of weeks ago the minister made a very good speech when introducing the bill on water control, there is not much indication that the federal government intends to move into this field.
The provinces are concerned about air pollution which can vary from one province to another. They are also concerned about pollution of our rivers and lakes by the cities which have not provided for the adequate treatment of the water dumped into these rivers and lakes by their sewage disposal systems. I spoke of this problem a few days ago, Mr. Speaker. I again want to put on record that the city of Montreal, with a population of 21 million, dumps 93 per cent of its sewage into the St. Lawrence River in an untreated state. Quebec city, which is represented by one of the leading ministers of this government, dumps 100 per cent of its sewage into the St. Lawrence River in an untreated state. Halifax follows a similar procedure. I am certain the municipal authorities of the cities to which I have referred are just as concerned about polluting the waters surrounding them as the mayors and representatives of other cities in Canada.

These cities are faced with tremendous financial problems. The proper treatment of sewage in the city of Montreal would cost approximately $100 million. We are all aware of the financial crisis being faced by the city of Montreal. This city has tremendously high local taxes and cannot afford to do the job which is required. This government has not shown any signs of introducing a program of grants or low cost loans to the city of Montreal to finance adequate sewage treatment facilities. 1 feel this is an illustration of this government's approach to the problems of the cities. No matter how important their problems are, they must be kept at arm's length from the federal government.
I was amused when I listened to the hon. member for Etobicoke (Mr. Gillespie) last night. He suggested that representatives of the municipalities should be present at these constitutional conferences. I think this is an excellent idea, but the hon. member should consider how that suggestion fits in with the Prime Minister's view that the cities are solely the creatures of provincial governments and, therefore, they have no right-indeed there is no need-for them to be present at federal-provincial conferences. Of course, they can attend these conferences if the provinces make arrangements for them to be part of their delegation, but the municipalities have no constitutional right as far as the Prime Minister and the federal government are concerned.
The problems which concern the people of Canada are the day to day bread and butter problems of work, housing, environment and a better life, qualitatively and materially. These are the problems which this government has put into the background. Although the legislation that we are being asked to deal with is important, it is not designed to improve the living conditions of the people of Canada. It is for this reason that there has been a lessening of interest in the constitutional problems of this country.
I urge the government to reconsider its position and to come to the constitutional conferences with the provinces with specific proposals. The people of Canada are not concerned whether the problems are solved by the federal, provincial or municipal governments. They are desirous of their problems being solved, their needs being looked after and not being put off to another day or year because one government or the other disclaims responsibility.
January 27, 1970

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) told us yesterday that we have to talk to each other quite frankly. I hope to follow his guidelines and speak as frankly as I can about the constitutional position which he put forward yesterday on behalf of his party and, to use his words, to do so without offence.
I must say that the performance of the Leader of the Opposition yesterday was curious and unconvincing. As a statement of his party's policy on the constitution, it was contradictory and self-defeating. Indeed, at times his contradictions verged on the brink of incoherence. He complained that Parliament had not been consulted on the constitutional reforms, the revision of the constitution. Well, Parliament is being consulted now. After he spoke, the nation was no wiser as to where his party stood on the great question of the constitution. It is regrettable from the point of view of reaching a consensus in the House that, having heard the Leader of the Opposition, no one is any wiser as to the stand taken by his party on essential constitutional issues. What has happened to the party of Sir John A. Macdonald, of Borden, Meighen, Diefen-baker, when it is silent in this great debate and has no stand to put before the House?
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
We thought this debate would afford us an opportunity to hear the views of the opposition. We thought the Leader of the Opposition would grasp the occasion to outline the position of his party. The fact is, we now know less than we did before. We thought we knew where he stood before he spoke, but after he spoke we were no longer certain. At one point he stated he was "not as confused as all that". His followers seemed to be grateful for this assurance, because that remark brought the first burst of applause from the opposition benches.
don't hear the Prime Minister applauding you.

speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext:
In spite of the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition or, indeed, because of it, I am convinced the government has followed the right course, first, in opening up the subject for debate at the urging of the provinces and, second, in seeking a national consensus, as well as in its assessment of the results achieved to date.
Canadian Constitution
The debate has been going on for two years. It has been made a public debate because of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) insistence that the people be made aware of what is going on. The Leader of the Opposition shouts: "Bring in the people." Well, the people have been in on this debate from the very beginning through the medium of television. For some reason, the Leader of the Opposition seems to be unaware, not only of the significance of the constitutional process, but also of the fact that the debate itself has been an open and continuing one. Now, he is showing a curious reluctance to grasp the fundamental issue before the House.
Parliament is being asked, or it will be later in the committee, to pronounce its views on vital issues concerned with constitutional reform and affecting Canadians from coast to coast. This is an opportunity for the Leader of the Opposition and his party to put on record their stand on these great issues.
All we heard from the Leader of the Opposition was a lugubrious lamentation. No doubt, this statement of his will be known as the "our days are numbered" speech. Matters of language rights, social rights, the distribution of powers, relations between senior levels of government, shared-cost programs, powers for dealing with regional disparity-these, together with a multitude of other considerations, have been brought out during the debate in a search for a national consensus. Surely, the process of bringing these issues before Canadians on the part of the Prime Minister should not, in the name of constructive criticism, be arbitrarily described, as it was by the Leader of the Opposition, as a total failure. The hon. gentleman stated that the federal-provincial meetings had demonstrated practically no progress.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition made an important statement yesterday. He said important things-important and wrong things. Anyone who has attempted to follow the progress of the constitutional discussion is bound to reach the conclusion that progress has, indeed, been made.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Backwards.

speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext:
I want to place on record for the benefit of members of the House and, I hope, of the public a list of what I believe to be important areas of progress since this process began.

January 27, 1970
Canadian Constitution
1.	There has been agreement between the Government of Canada and the provincial governments to enter upon a complete review of the constitution. At the first conference, in 1968, there was agreement to examine highly important questions including the official languages, fundamental rights, the distribution of powers, regional disparity, amending procedures, the mechanism of federal-provincial relations, and so on. Later, at the second conference, it was agreed to undertake a comprehensive review of the constitution of Canada, including the possibility of adopting an entirely new constitution.
2.	A second step, and one which I believe to be of great importance, was the establishment of the machinery necessary to undertake this review. It was brought about by setting up a continuing conference composed of the Prime Minister and the premiers, together with a continuing committee, or secretariat, of officials to assist them.
3.	The third item I would place before the House is the adoption of a firm position on language rights. Hon. members will recall the atmosphere in which the conference of February, 1968 was held, and I was relieved, as, indeed, many people were, including the participants, when the conference agreed to recognize, as proposed by the Commission on Biculturalism and Bilingualism and as a matter of equity, that French-speaking Canadians outside Quebec should have the same rights as English-speaking Canadians in Quebec. The late Daniel Johnson attended that conference and I remember his comments following the adoption of that principle by the conference.
4.	There has been agreement that reduction of regional disparities is an objective of confederation. There was agreement that the federal government should have the power to alleviate regional disparities as they affected the income of individuals, the quality of economic development and the standards of public services. Undoubtedly this agreement for the inclusion of the objectives of the elimination of regional disparities should be made part of the preamble to the constitution. There was an agreement further, as I read the proceedings, that if the difficulty of effecting the supremacy of Parliament and judicial review could be overcome, there would be an obligation imposed to achieve the goal of the elimination of regional disparity.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Remember, too, what the premier of Nova Scotia said of the conference when he dis-

cussed this issue. I looked it up last night. He was debating, at the conference, the inclusion of this objective in a new constitution. He said as follows:
I believe the Inclusion of a type of statement in the preamble we have been talking about, (namely the eradication of regional disparity) as an objective of confederation is a great step forward, accompanied by providing powers which would enable that objective to be followed and pursued. We have certainly got something in the constitution we have never had before or will have when we have that new constitution.
That is the view of the premier of Nova Scotia and his colleagues from the Atlantic provinces as well as elsewhere in Canada who felt that the inclusion of this goal in the constitution was an objective of paramount importance. When it was achieved, the premier of Nova Scotia said it was a great step forward. I wonder how he feels now that his one-time colleague from Nova Scotia describes his efforts as practically no progress at all. That is number four.
5.	Number five was an agreement at the constitutional conference that the national capital should reflect the two cultural groups of Canada. That is rather important to many people, including members of this House of Commons. It was agreed in February 1969 that steps must be taken to ensure that the two official languages and the cultural values common to all Canadians were recognized in the capital region, so that all Canadians may have a feeling of pride, participation in and attachment to their capital. This was a step forward.
6.	Number six was agreement in principle on powers of taxation. This has been totally ignored in the debate so far, but the working session of the constitutional conference in June 1969 generally agreed on the principle of access by both federal and provincial governments instead of the principle of allocation. There was general agreement on powers of taxation reached at this conference.
7.	Number seven was agreement in principle on the spending powers of Parliament. It is surprising that the Leader of the Opposition did not speak of the very definite movement toward reconciliation on this important issue of the use of the federal spending power in fields of exclusive provincial jurisdiction.
I read the proceedings again. There was a definite movement towards a consensus and it was agreed, even by Quebec, that Parliament should have the power to make conditional grants to provinces, subject to a formula to determine a consensus and for compensation to non-participating provinces.
January 27, 1970

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Even a glacier has movement.

speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext:
Well, that is a very important movement. No wonder the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) is so sensitive because he, too, joined last night in the unfounded allegations of his leader that no progress had been made. Even that progress would justify these conferences because it does provide a developing consensus on one of the issues that has bedevilled, at least in the minds of many, the whole field of federal-provincial relations.
The federal government, through its spending power has moved into fields of exclusive provincial jurisdiction with shared cost programs. Here is a method proposed by which a consensus could be reached before that power would be used. That is number seven.
8.	Number eight was at the last conference, an initiation of consideration of income security and social services. That began with the third conference in December 1969 and will continue. I want to come back to the question of social services and income security. It is surprising that the members of the NDP would suggest that there has been no attention to social needs when the first document in the field of the distribution of powers was directed to the whole question of how the power in the field of income security and social services should be exercised between the government of Canada and the governments of the provinces.
The NDP accuses us of not dealing with social needs at the constitutional conference. The Leader of the Opposition asked, "why have you chosen welfare?" We have chosen it, however, and I want to say something more about it.
9.	The ninth achievement that I would lay down is that, as in all processes involving bargaining, there have been a lot of issues clarified and a lot of positions placed on the table. Positions have been taken by the provinces and by the federal government. The federal government insofar as issues already dealt with, had made its position fully known, the Quebec government has made its position known totally, and many of the provinces are laying their positions on the table as well.
To suggest, as has been suggested by the Leader of the Opposition and the member for Peace River, that no progress has been made in this effort is to fly in the face of the facts and to take a position that can only be based on total misinformation or blind partisanship.
Canadian Constitution
No one else has done that. Certainly no premier. Most certainly, the premier of Nova Scotia, would not line up behind the opposition and say there has been no progress at all.
The Leader of the Opposition came close to, suggesting that the federal-provincial conference, as an instrument of constitutional revision, should be junked altogether, that the provinces should be left out. This seemed to-be what he suggested in one or two places in his speech. It may be, he said, that the committee will decide that the method chosen by the Prime Minister and the government is not working and that another method of approach, perhaps one quite substantially different, might well produce results. It is evident to all of us, he said, that the method of federal-provincial conferences is not working,, and he invited the committee to junk it and find something else. I read the speech not once, but twice, and it left an area of doubt as to whether the Leader of the Opposition really believed that the provinces should be included at all in this whole process of constitutional reform.
I conclude this part of my speech by asking the Leader of the Opposition if he believes that the nine areas I have discussed are meaningless, useless and trivial, and that no progress at all has been made?
The Leader of the Opposition moved on to ask why we selected welfare rather than pollution, for example, for discussion at the constitutional conference. I am sure that if we had selected pollution as the first item in the field of distribution of powers, he would have asked why we had not chosen the important field of social welfare.
I want to move into the subject a little bit by asking the Leader of the Opposition whether he is an adherent of the school of the instant constitution, and that someday there will arrive on his desk by some miracle a full blown constitution with all subject matters delineated perfectly for him. Does he believe that the re-writing of the Canadian constitution involves a consideration of each subject matter, a discussion of each power and a decision on each power as to whether it ought to be exercised exclusively by the federal or provincial governments, or concurrently, or in some other manner? If that is the answer, as I think it is, then one must start somewhere and choose among the many important and complex areas such as income, security and social services, economic growth, pollution, housing, urban transportation, the credit system, the financial markets, education,

January 27, 1970
Canadian Constitution
resources management, labour relations and manpower, culture and communication, to mention some of the issues that have to be resolved in this process.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. minister but I am afraid his time has expired. Is there unanimous consent to allow the minister to continue?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let me say on a point of order, as one who has become involved with the number of speakers for today, that we are going to run into extreme difficulty. We have a long list of important speakers. May I suggest that each speaker be allowed to take one or two minutes to complete his remarks or finish a sentence or two, but no more. I appreciate that this courtesy was granted yesterday, but I feel we will be in trouble if we allow more than an extra minute or two.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: All I can do at this point is ask whether there is agreement to allow the hon. minister to continue. The minister might bear in mind the recommendations of the hon. member.

speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree that there is a time limitation. I thank hon. members for their courtesy in granting a minute or two, but I believe I should rest my case at this stage and let other hon. members, possibly some of the leaders in the opposition, indicate what their position is on some of these points.

Mr. Speaker, when one enters the debate at this stage one finds himself in the rather unenviable position of having to discuss matters which have already been very thoroughly discussed by the speakers who have preceded him, all of whom are very knowledgeable on the subject matter of the resolution. I am not quite sure at this point whether I should include the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) in that category. I must say I was very disappointed because I thought, as a minister of the crown, he would make some valuable contribution to the subject matter of this resolution rather than devote all of his time to a criticism of the points put forward yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield).
I listened yesterday with a great deal of interest to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). As he led off this debate, I was

forced to come to the conclusion that this resolution is on the order paper today and is being debated in this house now, not because the Prime Minister of Canada has any burning desire to present a revised constitution to the people of Canada, but rather and perhaps only because oppoisition parties in this House and many of the premiers in Canada have been pressuring him now for many years to do this very thing. It is only now, at this late date, that he has got around to doing it. Let me quote in support of that proposition from his speech of yesterday. We find at page 2811 of Hansard that he is recorded as having said:
Indeed, parties of the opposition have pressed the government for many months, and even over a period of two sessions, to set up this committee. I believe that this reflects on the part of hon. members a very great desire of participating in the constitutional debate taking place in this country.
He does not point out that he has any great desire to press this matter or to take part in this debate.
Again, at page 2812 of Hansard, in speaking of the conference called by Premier Robarts, the Prime Minister is recorded as stating:
Not only did we not participate in the 1967 conference, but in the years prior to that we had taken the very clear position that the constitution was not the most urgent thing to be dealt with, that there were many problems facing Canadians which could be dealt with under the British North America Act. Although we were not prepared to discuss the subject, we urged the provinces and the public at large to regard these exercises with a certain amount of deliberation.
To me, that is a very clear indication that had it not been for pressure put on the Prime Minister and the Government of Canada by opposition parties in this House, and had it not been for the pressure put on him by the premiers of Canada, this resolution would never perhaps have appeared on the Order Paper, or at least not for a long time. I suggest that the Prime Minister of Canada need not be afraid of constitutional amendment as such, and he particularly need not believe that by introducing amendments to the constitution he is breaking new ground.
History tells us, if we examine it, that during the years from 1774 to 1867, during the period that Canada was under British rule, the British Parliament saw fit to adopt four different constitutions. From 1774 to 1791, we had the Quebec Act. From 1791 to 1840 we had the constitutional Act. From 1840 to 1867 we were governed by the Act of Union, and from 1867 to the present time we have been governed by the British North America Act. Let me point out to the Prime
January 27, 1970

Minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that since the British North America Act was enacted in 1867 we have had at least 30 constitutional amendments.
The constitution is not an eternal document and it was never intended as such. It is indeed an important document, and certainly one which we must adhere to and respect while it is in effect. But there is nothing so sacrosanct about it that it cannot, and indeed should not, be changed when it ceases to fit in with the needs of the times, or when it ceases to do the job it was originally intended to do. Things have changed since 1867. For example, the relationships between the federal and provincial governments have changed, and at least certain elements of the constitution by reason of these changes are now in need of review.
Yesterday the Prime Minister said that a great deal of preparatory work must go into this matter of constitutional change and amendment. I agree with that statement. This is certainly not a job which can be undertaken lightly. All aspects of constitutional change must be looked at and looked at very carefully, but they need not all necessarily be looked at at once. 1 suggest that priorities should be set up.
I agree that the British North America Act is a rather closely knit document and that one section of it is more or less interrelated with the other, but that does not necessarily rule out the advisability of first considering those parts of the document-and there are some- which already have been the source of discontent between the provinces and the federal government. One of those sources of discontent, and perhaps one of the more prominent ones, is the spending power of the federal government-the power of the federal government to make grants of any kind in areas considered exclusively provincial jurisdiction.
For example, I have in mind health and welfare, education, roads and things like these which are ordinarily considered to be matters exclusively within provincial jurisdiction. There is an element of uncertainty as to whether or not the federal government has the power to grant money to the provinces for these particular things. This uncertainty must be clarified as quickly as possible in respect of any constitution which may be drawn up. I suggest that the spending powers of the federal government must be clearly and unequivocally set out so that there can be 21611-43
Canadian Constitution
no question but that the government of Canada constitutionally is free to help the poor provinces financially.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration said this is now mentioned in the preamble. He made a great to-do about how much had been accomplished so far. I would point out to the minister that these matters have been pressed on the federal government by the premiers of the provinces of Canada now for some three or four years, and up until now no concrete action has been taken by the government of the country to bring these matters before the House of Commons. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration even bragged about how much this government has done in the line of constitutional amendments. It must be very definitely set out that this Parliament will have the power constitutionally to make grants to the poorer provinces of Canada even in those areas which are now considered to be areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction.
Sections 91, 92 and 93 of the British North America Act enumerate the respective exclusive powers of the Parliament of Canada and the provincial legislatures. Sections 92 and 93 specify and detail the matters upon which this Parliament may not legislate. Section 91 sets out those matters upon which the provincial legislatures may not legislate. Section 91, for example, reserves to the Parliament of Canada-and this is specifically written into the section-such matters as post offices, defence, fisheries, banking, the criminal law and so on. As a matter of fact, there are some 28 items enumerated in that section as being the exclusive right of the Parliament of Canada. Sections 92 and 93, on the other hand, reserve some 20 or more items to the provincial legislatures only. Right now the battle between the provinces and the federal government-and there is a battle-is over the distribution of federal subsidies to the provinces. I suggest, in the interest of the provinces, especially the poorer provinces, this is a matter which must first be clarified; that is, whether or not the government of Canada has the right to divert money to the provinces in respect of matters which under the British North America Act are now matters of exclusive provincial jurisdiction.
Section 91 1A reserves to the Parliament of Canada the right to make laws respecting public debts and property. This has been interpreted by the Supreme Court of Canada as giving to Parliament the power to grant

January 27, 1970
Canadian Constitution
sums of money to the provinces. That decision was appealed to the Privy Council. The Privy Council cast some very serious doubt as to whether, under our present constitution, the Parliament of Canada may divert money for these purposes. I should like to read very briefly from the judgment delivered by the Privy Council. It is found in 1937 Appeal Cases at page 366. This is what the Privy Council said:
But assuming that the Dominion has collected by means of taxation a fund, it by no means follows-
Listen to this:
-that any legislation which disposes of it is necessarily within Dominion competence. It may still be legislation affecting the classes of subjects enumerated in Sec. 92 and, if so, would be ultra vires. In other words, Dominion legislation, even though it deals with Dominion property, may yet be so framed as to invade civil rights within the Province or encroach upon the classes of subjects which are reserved to provincial competence.
Interpreted strictly, this decision means that Parliament absolutely cannot legally make grants of any kind in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction. This is what the Supreme Court decision says.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Leader of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Surely not; that is not what it says.

That is what it says. It says, for example, this would mean, if we go by the provisions of the British North America Act and the decision of the Privy Council, that strictly speaking federal funds cannot be diverted, for example, to education, welfare, highways and civil rights. I agreed that this is being done, and certainly the provinces are not taking any exception to it. I am afraid, however, that if this is not clarified immediately in our constitution, some day some government-I am not suggesting this government-may say, "We do not need to give you any money because the constitution says that, strictly speaking, we should not give it to you". This would be very much to the disadvantage of the poorer provinces of Canada.
Let us not forget that today we live in a federal state. All of us, no matter in what province we may happen to live, are Canadians. Each of us is entitled to enjoy the same essential public services that are being enjoyed by other citizens of Canada in the richer provinces. Unfortunately, however, the tax raising potential of our provinces differs greatly and this difference arises out of the marked difference in the level of income across this country.

I should like, if I may, to cite one or two
examples to show that this is actually the case. Listen to this. The average weekly wage in Canada is $114. In the Atlantic area it is $91.37. I wonder how many members know what it is in Prince Edward Island. In Prince Edward Island, it is $75.97, which is $38.06 below the Canadian average. This compares to the Canadian average of $114. Every winter in my province between 15 per cent and 20 per cent of the people are unemployed. These figures are from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. Half the farmers of Prince Edward Island have a gross income- not net-of $2,500 a year. As an indication of how heavily dependent we are on Ottawa I wish to point out that right now 62 per cent of our gross provincial revenue comes from the government of Canada.
Certainly, as one of the poorer provinces of Canada we cannot take any chance in respect of whether or not the Government of Canada has the constitutional right to transfer funds to the extent of 62 per cent of our revenue in order to help us. We have a total direct and guaranteed debt in Prince Edward Island of $107,635 thousand. That is a per capita debt of $970. This is one of the highest per capita debts in Canada. I suggest, in considering amendments to the constitution, the preservation of linguistic rights, revisions of the Senate and Supreme Court, the incorporation into the constitution of a bill of human rights and all such things are tremendously important, but there is nothing more important to the constitution than a guarantee that all the people of Canada will be able to enjoy the same essential public services irrespective of the provinces in which they happen to live. Canadian society must have no second class citizens. We cannot afford to have second class citizens in this country.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
In the examples I cited I set out very clearly I think that we in the Atlantic area, by reason of the fact that we do not have the same means of earning income as people in other parts of Canada,-not that we do not want to or are not anxious to work-cannot contribute to our provincial treasuries to enable them in turn to provide us with all our essential public services. We must have financial help from Ottawa, and I say that this help must be guaranteed in our constitution. Let us leave no doubt about it. I would suggest also that in considering amendments to the constitution we must give high priority to ensuring that there is absolutely no doubt
January 27, 1970

Canadian Constitution
that the Parliament of Canada has the right to transfer to the provincial governments money that can be used for things which are ordinarily matters under provincial jurisdiction. This is part of regional development.
We hear the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) making a big to-do about all that this government will do on behalf of regional development, but nothing has been done yet. Action must be taken immediately by his department or by some department of the federal government to reduce the gap between the rich and the poor provinces of Canada. This is a national problem and there is need for a national program to correct it. This is the reason I say that one of the highest priorities must be given to amending the constitution in such a way as to allow the federal government unequivocally, and without any doubt, to transfer moneys to the provinces. Therefore, I say that in any new constitution the spending power of the government of Canada must be clarified to provide, without any shadow of doubt, the federal government with the right to help the poor provinces. The federal government must retain that power to help the poor provinces.
As I said before, there must be an equalization of opportunity for all Canadians, irrespective of the province in which they live. There is no room in our Canadian society for great disparities between the opportunities available to individual Canadians no matter where they live. Reasonable standards of living for all Canadians must be maintained, and in amending our constitution we must make sure of this.
This principle was recognized by our former prime minister, the Right Hon. Lester Pearson when in 1968 he addressed the federal-provincial conference. This is what he said:
We believe that the government of Canada must have the power to redistribute income, between persons and between provinces, if it is to equalize opportunity across the country. This would involve, as it does now, the right to make payments to individuals, for the purpose of supporting their income levels-old age security pensions, unemployment insurance, family allowances-
There is no question about that because they have been provided by the constitution. He went on to say:
*-and the right to make payments to provinces, for the purpose of equalizing the level of provincial government services. It must involve, too, the powers of taxation which would enable the federal government to tax those best able to contribute to these equalization measures. Only in this way can the national government contribute to the equalization of opportunity in Canada, and thus supplement and support provincial measures to this end.
21611-43i
The whole point I am attempting to make is that our constitution must guarantee to the federal government the right to do these very things which the Right Hon. Mr. Pearson outlined to the conference in 1968. This is a matter of immediate urgency, one that must be attended to at once. I, therefore say, despite what the Minister of Manpower and Immigration said a few minutes ago about all the preambles in the constitution and about how much debate there has been on this matter, let us get on with the job immediately. Let us draft a constitution which will ensure both a strong federal government and also strong provincial governments, each with access to sufficient fiscal resources-and this is important-to meet their proper responsibilities, and each operating in a fashion that does not impair the freedom of the others.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, among the tasks we have to perform and the challenges we shall have to meet in the years to come, finding solutions to constitutional problems is of paramount importance. I have deemed it to be normal, and indeed my duty as a French-speaking Canadian, to participate in this debate, without claiming to bring final solutions, but solely with a view to offering my services.
As a federal member from a Quebec riding, I have long been interested in constitutional matters, and although I have had the honour of sitting in the nation's Parliament for less than two years so far, I believe it is possible for us to sit at the same table and, notwithstanding our political affiliations, to find a harmonious and effective solution agreeable to all Canadians.
Institutions are, in a sense, the mirror of the times when they are born and brought into operation. They reflect the various forms that man gives to society, according to his concept of organized life and of the objectives which should be aimed at. Because institutions reflect ideas and needs more or less linked with certain periods in history, they are constantly exposed to changes, as are the realities which inspired their creation.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Federalism does not escape that law of evolution. One can even assert that owing to the greater participation of citizens in public

January 27, 1970
Canadian Constitution
affairs, which is demanded by the complexity of its structures, the federal system is, more than any other type of political society, aware of the economic and social evolution, and it is also more apt to find the necessary solutions.
Federalism varies with times and countries, offering a wide variety of solutions consistent with its basic needs. The 19th century, which saw the rise and strengthening of the first modern federal systems, offers more than one form of federalism.
At the present time, a score of states, among which seven of the eight largest countries of the world are to be found, live under a federal system. There are only two with an identical constitution. However, it is a fact acknowledged by all: namely that Germany and the United States, which at present have a federal system, enjoy the world's highest standard of living. It is therefore easy to conclude that, by itself, federalism can be a source of wealth or poverty according to whether people accept or refuse to apply it as it should be applied.
Federalism is certainly not beyond the reach of violent crises because some federations have broken up during the last decade. However, thanks to the close relationships which the parties to a federative state normally maintain between themselves, they can generally find before it is too late the solutions likely to prevent the downfall of their association. As long as an institution is successful in adapting to new realities and operating efficiently, without going against its character, it has every chance of overcoming internal conflicts and surviving changes imposed by circumstances.
I believe the time has come for us to stop throwing words around and to take concrete action. As Canadians of various ethnic origins, are we willing to co-operate and to accept each other as equal partners? It is not incumbent only on me or on my colleagues to answer, but on the whole population.
For some time, I have been hearing from some opposition members innuendoes which would indicate that they do not look favourably upon French-speaking Canadians actually assuming their part in Parliament. I would like to know what they think exactly. I wish they would stop talking about Quebec and French-speaking Canadians. What I am interested in is what they think and what means they are ready to take to save national unity.
We French-speaking Canadians have given clear proof of our willingness to work to the limit of our strength to preserve this country,
[Mr. Marceau.l
but we are not ready to go on unless we are regarded as first class citizens. I feel that most hon. members, on the government side or in the opposition, would like such effort to be made by all equally, but I do not appreciate the innuendoes of some of my colleagues in the opposition, who should speak their minds. If they are not satisfied with this government, if they take offence because French Canadians are playing a leading part and if they do not trust them, they should say so. But if, on the other hand, they are really willing to work, they should give us some proof to that effect.
Yesterday, my hon. friend the member for York South (Mr. Lewis) mentioned, as an example, an incident which occurred in Quebec and from which certain people might draw erroneous conclusions. He said that the Quebec government had refused Englishspeaking Canadians another English school. I wish to say to my hon. friend that if, following his example, I tried to find out how the minorities of other provinces have been treated, I would have a lot to say. As a matter of fact, my hon. friend, for whom I have great respect, is intelligent enough to recognize that, in Quebec, the minorities are better treated than anywhere else, and that, if all minorities in Canada were treated like the ones in Quebec, the problems facing us today would not exist.
It may not be wise to be forever looking back to the past instead of looking forward to the future, but one must remember that confederation, as history teaches us, has not been, like the Proclamation of Independence of the United States, the dramatic result of a fight for liberation, but rather the outcome of hard discussions carried out during more than three years by parliamentarians who were not threatened by any war, either at home or abroad.
In Upper Canada, which was the inspiring centre of the system inaugurated in 1967, people had been complaining for a long time about the powerlessness of the two majorities system created by the Act of 1840. They were complaining all the more bitterly since the population of Upper Canada, indifferent to the rights of the majority as long as its population was lower than that of Lower Canada, suddenly awakened, as soon as it had the majority, to the democratic seductions, that of the greatest number. The political leaders of Upper Canada were also concerned about the rise of the American power. They could not think of any other way to face this peril
January 27, 1970

except by uniting in a single Dominion all the British colonies scattered in North America.
As a matter of fact, what presided over the drafting and the signature of the confedera-tive pact? On this point, history does not say much, but I think that I am expressing the truth in saying that English-speaking Canadians felt that on the main points they had kept what was essential to them, especially the guarantee of a strong central government. French-speaking Canadians on the other hand were convinced that they had preserved for the future what in their view could not be left to the care of a central government.
To both sides history has brought many disappointments. Those who had dreamed of an all powerful central government were to be deceived for instance by some decisions of the Privy Council which tended to confirm and to extend the sovereignty of the provincial governments and by the everlasting vitality of a strong autonomist movement in Quebec.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Those who had dreamed of a central government respectful of the authority of the provinces and of the rights of minorities often had to face one which dared not fulfil its constitutional duties towards minorities and which much too often was unscrupulous regarding the sovereignty of the provinces.
The present government is the first one, it seems to me, that really concerns itself about the protection of the rights of minorities, the recognition of biculturalism and bilingualism and the defence of provincial rights. If the present government seeks to protect those fundamental rights, we must not be satisfied with temporary conditions.
We want-and I think that I am thus expressing the views of the majority of Frenchspeaking Canadians-those conditions to become permanent, we want them to be written down, in order to prevent the recurrence of past events.
It was the wish in 1867 to merge two separate wills in a new one. Sir Georges-Etienne Cartier had spoken in this connection of a new political nationhood. The strongest community invited to unite its political destiny did it unreservedly. The weakest community, however, did not adhere to the new plan without some reserves, being almost equally divided between two currents of thought. The tendency in favour of a full commitment in the federal experience has generally won during the past century the support of French Canadians at federal elections.
Canadian Constitution
The other tendency, with various degrees of intensity, has found its main center of action in Quebec. This ambivalence has certainly been detrimental to Quebec and often delayed progress in Canada.
I am the first one to recognize that Quebec has failed to appreciate federalism. Hon. members from Quebec have the responsibility to show federalism under its true light and to make French-speaking Canadians understand that this system is in a position to help them provided they accept it fully and not half-heartedly.
It is well to blame those who do not try to make federalism better known but I think that it is up to us as members of political parties and members of the House, whatever our political affiliations, to make real federalism known.
That is what we are doing now in the province of Quebec. Hon. members from Quebec are touring the province to explain, to the young in particular, the advantages federalism is likely to bring them.
We agree that federalism is not perfect. I was listening recently to a member from the Ralliement creditiste talking about the Liberal party. I wish to point out to him that this idea has not been authored by the Liberal party and that if he wants to join us, he would be welcomed, but on one condition-if he is able to accept it-that he will not turn the future of the country into a political issue and that he will truly deal with the things that unite us instead of the ones that divide us.
Mr. Speaker, will the hon. member for Lapointe allow me to ask him a question?
Gladly, Mr. Speaker, provided it is not too long.
Would the hon. member give the names of those who travel throughout Quebec and Canada explaining the nature of the constitution?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend, whom I hold in high esteem, does not read the papers, although I see one before him just now. If he looked for information, he could easily find out that there is nothing secret about what we are doing. Good Liberals travel throughout the province in order to inform people and if he wants to find out their names, he can easily do so.

How many of these people are there? What are their names?

January 27, 1970
Canadian Constitution

Mr. Speaker, I feel that it would not be appropriate to mention the names right now but after my speech, if the hon. member wants to come to me I shall be pleased to give him the names of those involved in this work.
They are all Liberals.
Naturally.
Naturally.

Mr. Speaker, we are in power and naturally, we are supposed as a responsible government to come to the aid of the population, and that is what we are doing. My hon. friend cannot blame us for that situation, and hon. members of the opposition cannot rail against the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) because he has personal views on the constitution. Were the members of the opposition to have views as original and as constructive as the Prime Minister's, the problem would perhaps be settled more easily. I find it somewhat odd to see people blame a man for showing leadership, expressing views, and building something, by saying precisely that he has no inventive ideas.
Of course, when one has no original ideas to offer, one can merely criticize those who have.
In the few minutes at my disposal, I would like to outline what our constitution should hold and express briefly a few basic ideas.
To my mind, the preamble to the Canadian constitution should outline a certain number of principles typical of its spirit and define its nature and aims so as to facilitate its interpretation. The main purpose of the constitution of a country is not merely to establish political structures and a form of government. It should also have an educational value. It must instil in the whole population feelings of pride and loyalty, be conducive to understanding and friendship, and favour full cooperation in the pursuit of a common ideal. It should be founded on certain essential premises-

I thank my hon. colleagues. I wish I could discuss this subject at length. I hope I shall have the opportunity to do so in the proposed committee I would like to see established.
Before concluding I should like to say that I have faith in the new committee, that will be set up to offer my full co-operation and, above all, to ask my English-speaking colleagues, whom I trust entirely, to have talks with us and to work for the unity of this country of which we are proud and which, we must recognize it, is envied by many others.

Mr. Speaker, in early fall when the session began I had the opportunity of asking that a debate be held on the constitution during this session. Today I am very glad to take part in this debate.
I have no hesitation at all in telling the House that I am in favour of a constitutional review. This is also an excellent opportunity for any member to voice his opinion, make suggestions and shed light on the problems and the difficulties confronting us. Having a better knowledge of these problems, I think we shall be more likely to solve them.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
First of all, I should like to mention that the constitution of 1867 is at times not satisfactory. It therefore has too often been a source of misunderstanding and conflict rather than an instrument of cohesion and harmony. It seems to us that respect for the fundamental law of the country is one of the first requirements of Canadian life. But the constitution must be such as to command this respect, as well through its nobility of thought as its clarity.
For the first time in their history, Canadians are undertaking to give themselves a wholly Canadian constitution, made in Canada, for Canadians. From this great undertaking must result, not only government institutions and regulations that are perfectly adapted to the present needs of our country, but also a new spirit and new habits of cooperation and solidarity.
As a member from Quebec, I might be inclined to speak more particularly of the Quebec responsibilities or difficulties within
January 27, 1970

that federal system. I hope the other members do the same for, to my mind, it is their duty to do so.
Quebec, which in our vast country is considered by the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission as the home of the French Canadian nation, has not only the right but the duty to find means of emancipation. Just as the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) did so brilliantly a moment ago, I invite all the members from Quebec to express their views that there might be a better understanding of the wishes and aspirations of Quebec as well as the means to which Quebecers can resort to feel secure in this large country and confident they are first-class citizens.
There have also been some things said about federal-provincial conferences. I believe such conferences are necessary even if they have not given so far the anticipated results. I hope their number will increase as they give the provincial premiers an opportunity to meet one another, to know and understand each other better and to accept more willingly the disparities that exist between the various provinces and regions.
Our position in the province of Quebec shows easily enough the special situation of French culture in Canada and in North America. If the French Canadians were a minority everywhere in Canada, including Quebec, cultural equality would be difficult to reach and the present concept of French Canada would be much different from what it is now.
The fact that 83 per cent of French-speaking Canadians are living in Quebec, where they represent 81 per cent of the population, allows them to develop their own institutions as well as an environment that suits their particular culture. That is where the chances for achieving cultural equality spring from, as indicated in the report of the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission, namely in subsections 83, 89 and 90.
Such equality is possible since a French Canadian society managed to be born, to thrive and to develop and also to acquire the distinct traits and institutions which contrive to make a true people-which cannot be said of any other ethnic minority in Canada.
While all governments should, to various degrees, do their best to bring about such equality, the demographic reality and the political and historical development of Canada will still invest the government of Quebec with special responsibilities in this respect, whether we like it or not.
Canadian Constitution
Obviously, the fact involves, for the future, recognition of a special status for the province of Quebec. However, Quebec should have all the necessary powers and means of action to go on assuming its responsibilities towards the French Canadian nation.
Nonetheless, Quebec does not object to the other provinces enjoying the same powers and means of action if they wish. The notion of a special status will appear only if the other provinces or some of them prefer to entrust the central government with or to discharge jointly with it the tasks that the province of Quebec must take upon itself by reason of its particular situation.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said yesterday that courage, patience and dedication will have to be exercised. I think that all hon. members are courageous. Patience, in the case of some of them, has limits. Dedication is called for, I think, when such a question is under discussion.
I have nevertheless the courage to talk about a certain political climate and to deal with the dissatisfaction of the people in my province. Dissatisfaction could also exist elsewhere.
On account of the economic conditions which are sometimes unfavorable, unemployment in Quebec has done great harm and is the cause of some discontent. It must be frankly said that such discontent is perhaps due to the reluctance of the Canadian Parliament to bring in certain amendments to the constitution.
This wavering on the part of Parliament has, in the last several years, prompted a number of Quebecers to believe that the separation of Quebec from the rest of the country would be advantageous for their province. I am not convinced of that, but I think it is necessary to tell things as they are, and we are already assured, on account of the dissatisfaction that prevails in Quebec, that when the next provincial election comes around, 10 per cent of the people will vote in favour of separation. This position reveals the extent of the need to review the constitution in order to enable the people of Quebec to believe in a better future and opportunities for emancipation, for the French Canadian nation and for all other Canadians, because such a future can be found in confederation.
The committee will certainly have to assume responsibility for making this Parliament aware that special arrangements will be necessary for Quebec, and for other regions as well. I feel sure that the committee, after

January 27, 1970
Canadian Constitution
consulting with representatives of all the provinces and with people who carry heavy responsibilities within certain municipalities, will recognize how important it is to obtain the participation of the people of Canada in order to determine the kind of constitution best suited to meet the requirements of all Canadians.
Hon. members should be asked not to be shocked when they hear from time to time that the province of Quebec intends to retain its French character.
Actually, they should stop being concerned when they hear that Quebec wants to establish French as its working language.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I readily recognize, as do all other Quebecers, that in Ontario English is the first language because the situation in that province demands it. French is being recognized as a second language.
The same situation prevails in Quebec where we want to keep our French language and increasingly to improve it. We are also prepared-as many Quebecers have proved it-to accept English as a second language.
These things must be said in the House, and I think that with a great deal of sincerity, we will finally convince not only most Canadians but all of them to accept the fact that the province of Quebec represents the French element in our bicultural country and that the other nine provinces will always keep English as their first language but will accept French as a second language, which makes me very happy.
The hon. member for Lapointe mentioned earlier that the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) had made about us what I would call an unpleasant reference. Having taken note of it I realized that I had not been the only one to notice it. Yesterday, the hon. member for York South said that in the province of Quebec, some people were concerned about the fact that, next year, 3,000 Englishspeaking students will be unable to be admitted to CEGEPs. I object to that statement and I cannot help but state my views in that respect.
The hon. member for York South stated, and I quote:
I deliberately cited this example of retrograde behaviour on the part of the government of Quebec to underline the difficulties which are now being created-
Certainly there are difficulties in the province of Quebec but they are surely not due to any ill-will on the part of the government.

I know the present premier of Quebec too well to say that he can be charged with preventing, through ill-will, the English-speaking students of Quebec from being admitted to CEGEPs.
Of course, since 1960, there has been in Quebec, in the field of education, such a rapid expansion that the government has been unable to build enough schools. But, in my opinion, if some English-speaking students of Quebec find it difficult to be admitted in the schools, the French-speaking students have as many difficulties when they want to register at the universities.
I have to make these remarks about the speech of the member for York South because I am convinced that the province of Quebec does not intend to do any harm whatsoever to the minorities. Far from it. Indeed, the past shows that Quebec always had much respect for its minorities and that it has always proved that all the minorities were welcome in Quebec.
I would like to mention especially that the committee should not forget to consult, first, the provinces. This practice of appointing commissions or committees for various inquiries has shown too often that the provinces were not taken into account and the central government has often been blamed, unfortunately, for taking decisions without previous consultation with the provinces.
The relations the government of Quebec has entered into now and then with some foreign countries, are also causing concern, as was mentioned yesterday.
To my mind, since Quebec is the home of the French Canadian nation, it must absolutely have contacts with some Frenchspeaking countries. I suppose this could be done in co-operation with the central government, which should show some understanding in this regard and recognize that a province such as ours ought to negotiate and sign agreements with the other French-speaking countries.
For years, members from Quebec and the government of that province have been asked what they really wanted. I think that for quite a while Quebec has been clear and precise about its intentions and its needs. In its recent brief on the constitution, it explained why it considered essential that the provinces have sole responsibility over social security. The coexistence of two governments prevents efficient planning in the field of social security, gives rise to the establishment of incon-
January 27, 1970

sistent programs and leads to administrative overlapping and wasting.
The whole social security provisions bear a direct relation to the culture of the people and enable them to express themselves collectively. The Quebec community can no more be deprived of its social security system than of its legal or educational systems.
The assigning of the entire responsibility of social security to the provinces can, through proper financial mechanisms, be consistent with a fair redistribution of income and the mobility of workers throughout Canada as well as with efficient economic policies.
The mechanism for the delegation of powers, the establishment of which has been proposed, will enable the provinces wishing to do so to entrust the central government with the discharge of some of those duties.
Quebec has no right to commit its future according to the wishes of a majority. Besides, I was blaming its authorities for leaving to the central government all responsibilities for the future of the French Canadian people.
The principles which must guide the originators of a healthy federal constitution are first the rational allocation of powers, then a joint action, with the possibility of exceptions, when the jurisdiction is not readily obvious, or when the motives of the various member states do not result from the same requirements or the same priorities.
That implies, on the one hand, a review of the allocation of exclusive jurisdictions under sections 91 and 92 of the present constitution, and, on the other hand, the establishment of a concurrent list on taxation and the distribution of public funds, with the possibility of exception for any province.
It will be enough to mention that such a notion of a federal constitution, while safeguarding almost the whole list of present federal powers, institutionalizes certain practices adopted until now by our governments, practices which, under foreseen conditions, seem to be much better juridical formulas than those found elsewhere, because they recognize, on the one hand, the principle of autonomy and, on the other, the principle of participation. Proving this would be beyond the scope of that section and, to be sure, only an entirely new constitution can reach this objective.
The constitutional documents of certain countries contain first class texts on the various subjects that have been mentioned. Germany, a federal state, has adopted a basic declaration of great interest. Italy, a unitary
Canadian Constitution
country with deeply-rooted regionalism, enshrines the principle of decentralization in her constitution. The USSR, a federal country with centralizing aims, grants her federated republics the acknowledgement of their cultural values in a manner probably unequalled in other texts. Australia, a federal country, offers an original formula for financing the states. The treaty of Rome, which may give rise to a federation, provides, from an economic standpoint, arrangements mostly derived from federalism while others represent interesting progress.
Mr. Speaker, I see that you are about to remind me that my time is up, but I still have one minute left.
The big advantage of a major overhaul of the constitution is that we shall be able to benefit by everything that has been done elsewhere, to digest it, to shape it to our own liking and to submit it to the nation for approval while adhering to the best principles and to the most efficient procedures. If Canada is not able to make very soon this effort of reflection and adaptation, it will have betrayed its past and gravely jeopardized its future.
The constitutional amendments which the committee will have to examine more closely may be classified into four categories of reforms: a clarification of the fiscal powers, in the light of the tasks with which the Quebec government must deal; the cultural equality between Canada's two linguistic communities both within the federal institutions and within those of the various provinces involved; the new distribution of powers between the government of Canada and that of Quebec which will enable the latter to fulfil its mission as the collective mainstay of the French Canadians and, by that very fact, to find once for all the link between Ottawa and Quebec; the formal acknowledgment of the rights of Quebec to conclude international agreements, after consultation with the government of Canada, in fields of provincial jurisdiction, and to participate in the work of the UN institutions specialized in those fields.
In reviewing the text of our constitution, we should take advantage of the occasion and express in modem language the general objectives of Canada, the jurisdictional basis for its administration and the distribution of powers between the two levels of government.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that we will effect these constitutional changes immediately which would contribute, if we act wisely, to the building of a fantastic country with well

January 27, 1970
Canadian Constitution
organized provinces where the emphasis is on co-ordination rather than federal centralization.
So, as the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) has pointed out, let us stop talking but let us work together and build a beautiful country.
