Mr. Speaker, like other members who have already taken part in this debate I welcome the establishment of this committee. I welcome it particularly because it marks the recognition that constitutional reform is above all a political question and it must ultimately be settled by political processes. Constitutional reform is not simply a question to be left to bureaucrats, to legal experts, or even to governments. It is a process which must involve the participation of the Canadian people as a whole. At the root of this question is the formation of our political institutions, the decision-making institutions of our government. That involves elaboration of the kind of values which we wish to have guide our community in taking decisions. It is pre-eminently a political question and not one that can simply be left to experts.
When I say this is a political question, that is not to say it must necessarily be dominated by partisan political considerations. I was a little dismayed yesterday in the House when it seemed to me there was a disposition on the part of some members taking part in the debate to look for fault, to try to find out where errors were, to search for places where they could stick something unpleasant on the government or opposition as the case might be. It seems to me that if the committee is to work well it must search for the common ground. It must pursue the question of the constitution with attempts at understanding rather than by making points in a partisan way.
Nevertheless, it is the political system which must represent, and the parties which must represent, the various views which can be taken of constitutional reform. This is the way in which the question must be taken to the people.
It is understandable that we should now be considering this question very seriously. It is platitudinous, but nevertheless true, that after

100 years the British North America Act is not particularly suitable to the needs of this country. It has been a constitution which has been less flexible in adapting to changing circumstances, partially because it has no formal amending procedure and partially because it has been subjected to court review, or constitutional review-taking place in a context far from this country-which has often led to decisions which could, at best, be described simply as bizarre.
We now face, at least in my part of the country, some impatience with the process of constitutional review. I think this is eminently understandable because, in an age of instant coffee, and instant television, people often demand instant solutions to complex problems. We must explain, and I think it is the obligation of political parties to explain, that these are rather complex questions, that there are divergent views in various parts of the country on how they are to be resolved and that there are no quick and easy solutions to complicated problems.
I hope the committee will get down to involvement with people. It is, I understand, to travel throughout the country and I hope that political parties will take this opportunity of clarifying where they stand on some of the fundamental questions. One of these questions is often described in short form as the question of "special status", but more accurately should be described as a question of whether one province or some provinces are to have substantial legislative and administrative powers which are different from those of the other provinces. I think the government party has taken a fairly clear position on that. The other parties, it seems to me, have not. There is the whole question of what the relationship of the federal government should be to the urban communities, the urban governments in our society. It seems to me the government party has not taken as clear a position, and has not explained as clearly as I would have liked, its position on that constitutional question. Obviously, that is going to be of enormous importance as we go throughout the country and find out how people in the cities regard the role of the federal government in relation to the municipal governments.
There is also the question of the Bill of Rights which, it seems to me, we often simplify enormously by pretending it is only a question of protecting the fundamental rights of our citizens. In fact, it is a question of transferring to the jurisdiction of the
January 27, 1970

Supreme Court an enormous power of interpretation in many areas of fundamental political importance to our society. We must ask ourselves, as men in public life, whether it is the proper function of the courts to come to a determination on what are essentially political questions. It may very well be so, but we should be clear in our minds that in discussing a Bill of Rights we are also discussing a transfer of political power to the Supreme Court.
Yesterday, as always, I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) who described the participation of the various politicians who took part in the constitutional conference as participation of men of good will. He went on to say that really we were wrong in looking at this question as one of competition for power between the provincial governments and the federal government. It is not, he said, a question of power between the federal government and the provinces that confronts Canada. In all respect, Mr. Speaker, that is exactly the question. It is a question of the basic distribution of powers between the federal and provincial governments in this country which is at the root of the constitutional question. And in the constitutional conference we discuss these powers not simply in the abstract; it is not powers in some void about which we are talking. It is the powers which the politicians who are discussing the issues themselves hold at this particular point in time.
It is very difficult in those circumstances to have politicians not suspicious about the presentation of points of view by the other politicians who are sitting around the table. There is a story, Mr. Speaker, of two Renaissance cardinals, both great schemers. One of them was unfortunately carried away by the plague. When the news was reported to the other cardinal he said: "Dead; I wonder what his motive was". Now, politicians are not quite as suspicious as that, Mr. Speaker, but they are nevertheless very suspicious of the kind of powers and the claims to powers which other politicians make. It seems to me, this fact redoubles the emphasis we must give to this committee, to the involvement of the public in the question of constitutional reform. For in the end I suspect that the politicians, naturally sensitive to their own position, are not going to come to any easy agreement about what the proper distribution of powers among them is. It will take involvement of the public, and a view by the public 21611-44*
Canadian Constitution
as to what those powers should be-and eventually some attempt to find out what the public feels in an explicit way,-to give the moral authority to constitutional change which we require. It is, in other words, a process that cannot be left simply to politicians. We must in an active way find out what the viewpoint of the public is.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that we should not face this task, which is a long task and an arduous task, a difficult task, with any sense of dismay. To my mind this country has, through the decade of the sixties, been going through a process-not so slow,-of the real birth of the Canadian identity and the Canadian community. It is a decade in which the country has begun to come to terms with itself. During our past 100 years we have often been able to escape our political problems. We have been able to concentrate on the development of our resources, and when groups and classes in society have been frustrated they have been able to move to other parts of the country and start life anew. But in the last ten years we have had a coming together, and a recognition therefore of the problems that we face in the coming together. We are, it seems to me, finally developing a really sound political structure, one which takes into account the necessity of reconciling the views, often divergent views, of the various parts of our country.
The formation of a new constitution is part of this process, a process which will give perspective and form to decisions of government, one which will ensure that in coming to its decision the government will take into account various viewpoints and various parts of this country. That is the task in which the committee will be engaged. It is a task which they should pursue with optimism and hope.

Mr. Speaker, if we had been discussing the constitution as short a time as a year ago, I might have found myself in agreement with those who lean toward amending the constitution to make a strong central government even stronger. I would probably also have been among those who felt changes in the constitution were unnecessary. But since that time I have seen the government's intent spelled out in legislation, and heard it expressed in speeches and statements of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and others. I have seen something of the economic confusion and hardship that has followed upon a strong, aggressive

January 27, 1970
Canadian Constitution
central government determined to force its will upon the various regions of this country.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I saw at first hand, as an official observer for my party at the recent federal-provincial conference, something of our Prime Minister's purpose. It is obvious that he wants a strong central government-not strong in the sense commonly understood in the past, but strong in the sense of a dominant and domineering central government that would control, not only the various regions of Canada but individual Canadians to a great extent in every aspect of their social and economic life. This is apparent from the federal government's demands and its reaction to the attitude of the provinces at recent constitutional conferences. It is also apparent in legislation passed and pending in Parliament.
It appears to me to be a strong possibility at least that, using the combined provisions of the Estate Tax Act already passed, and the proposals in the white paper on tax reform yet to come, the government will effectively reduce individual Canadians to easily controlled and easily manipulated economic emits. The net effect of such a combination of legislation will be to eliminate small businesses and small businessmen, and to prevent the creation of any reservoirs of individual capital so necessary for small business and power.
Other legislation, notably the proposed measure dealing with investment, will shackle business to government so that business decisions, even decisions concerning future investment, would be at the control of the central authority. When that day comes, Canada may well be, in everything but name, an authoritarian socialist state. There will be little purpose then debating the constitutional balance between Ottawa and the provincial capitals. Canada will be a monolithic unitary state, no matter what the constitution says or provincial governments may claim. To phrase it bluntly, Mr. Speaker, I believe that if the plans of this government are realized we will have a very strong central government authority verging on dictatorship.
To achieve this, Parliament may be progressively downgraded and pushed aside and the provinces bound even more closely in Ottawa's web by means of forced economic dependency, while individual Canadians would be reduced to ciphers. The country is to be governed by a small group of non-elect-ed and non-responsible people, dominated by the Prime Minister of the day.

There has been some talk recently about our adopting the United States form of presidential government. If we are not careful, we will be beyond the point of being able to exert a choice. Before we know it we could end up having a president, with all the powers of the United States president but without any of the checks and balances that restrain the holder of that office from exercising wilful and tyrannical power. I have said I believe this is the aim of the government. I would like to emphasize that I did not mean this was necessarily the aim of the government party as a whole. I speak only of the executive.
It has been obvious, almost from the time of the 1968 election, that many members of the government party were unhappy with the manner in which they were being led. Today, we are hearing more and more the voices of dissent from government ranks. In the circumstances, this may be the very worst time at which to discuss constitutional change. We may find ourselves asking who speaks for whom? However, if it is the will of the House to establish a committee to study this question, there are two areas that I would like to see given priority. These are constitutional safeguards against excessive assumption of power by the executive and safeguards to ensure the provinces the means and the exclusive right to deal with matters within their stated jurisdiction.
Such safeguards should also ensure that never again can a central government in Canada use economics as a means of imposing its will on defenceless provinces. We must make it impossible for the federal government to use financial coercion and turn the weaker provinces into financial peons. The unfortunate fact today is that the federal government, in one way or another, has saddled the provinces with a variety of welfare, health and educational programs that are poorly framed, ill-timed and vastly expensive to operate.
This might be one thing if our national economy had continued on the up-beat without soft spots or pauses. But with inflation ravaging the national economy, trade in many basic areas in the doldrums, unemployment and the cost of living soaring, the provinces are in trouble. Today, we are seeing the law of the jungle operating in the field of public finance. The battle, as ever, goes to the strong. The federal government has grabbed the lion's share of tax revenue, leaving the provinces and their dependent municipalities
January 27, 1970

committed to huge expenditures and payments with only an over-burdened and inadequate share of the tax base upon which to raise the funds necessary.
I believe our constitution should provide safeguards against such dog-eat-dog economics and ensure fair shares for all levels of government commensurate with their degree of responsibility to the people of Canada. The more I see of our country today and the more I consider our current problems, the higher goes my regard to the Fathers of Confederation. They were shrewd, practical men who brought a minimum of emotion and a maximum of ingenuity and common sense to their task of providing a constitutional base for a new nation. Their assessment of Canada holds good today in my judgment. It was a nation of regions then and it is a nation of regions today.
Because they appreciated this fact, they provided that matters of the greatest regional concern be administered by regional or provincial governments. This was no accident. This was no compromise. This was not something confined only to the much smaller Canada of that day. This was an inspired method of providing flexibility in the constitutional and political field. I am convinced it is more of this flexibility that we need today, not less. The federal government has become progressively more involved in such fields as health, welfare and education, all of which are exclusively within the ambit of the provincial administrations. I believe they were deliberately placed there-and rightly so. They should be allowed to remain there now.
The federal government should confine itself simply and solely to providing what assistance is needed by individual provinces to keep their health, welfare and educational standards at or near a national level. I believe it is essential that the provinces have sufficient financial resources to enable them to establish and support their own set of priorities. No strings whatever should be attached to the financial assistance they are given. Their own citizens may be relied upon to police them. We may be sure, in these days of almost instantaneous information, that the people of any given province will know what others are receiving and will compel their government to give them the same, if they judge that their ability to carry such services is great enough.
If the people-the taxpayers-do not think that they can carry the load, it should not be imposed on them. It should not be imposed on
Canadian Constitution
them particularly by pressure exerted by some group of public servants who happen to cherish enthusiasm for some specific plan of social welfare. It seems obvious to me that democratic government must be a vehicle whereby people can govern themselves as they wish. In a country of widely differing regions such as ours, this means freedom of choice at the regional level. In a democracy there cannot be a mandate for any small group to tell the people what they should have.
It should not be difficult to arrive at an acceptable formula within the constitution that would provide unconditional federal grants as a matter of right to provinces requiring assistance in discharging their constitutional responsibilities. The financial status of any province and its potential for tax and other revenue can, today, be forecast with reasonable accuracy. Balanced against its requirements under the constitution, a figure for unconditional federal grants could then be calculated. Such a system, protected against manipulation or abuse by the constitution, would permit both levels of government to do their job without the continual bickering and bargaining that goes on today. It would effectively prevent the federal government from encroaching upon provincial fields of responsibility and leave full initiative and decision in these fields to the appropriate authority.
The massive sums of money now involved in this question of the Canadian provinces discharging their constitutional responsibilities greatly aggravates the situation and this aggravation will grow rapidly in the years immediately ahead. In 1967, the total expenditure of all governments on health, welfare and education was in excess of $10 billion. The Economic Council of Canada has estimated that, by 1975, this expenditure will have risen to about $19 billion annually. On the basis of these figures it is clear that, in 1967, the Canadian government spent about 16 per cent of the gross national product in areas strictly within provincial jurisdiction. If, as is forecast by the Economic Council, the GNP reaches the $100 billion mark by 1975, this percentage will have risen to the about 20 per cent of the GNP at that time. This gives you some idea of the magnitude of the financial question in relation to the constitution about which I have been talking. If we consider it wise that government expenditure not exceed 35 per cent, or so, of the gross national product then I think you can see how important this is.

In 1967, the federal, provincial and municipal governments spent a little better than $4 billion on education. According to the Economic Council this amount will more than double by 1975. The most important feature of these figures, however, is that the overwhelming proportion of these education costs will be for elementary and secondary schools, the principal educational responsibility of the provinces. If they are not provided the financial muscle to handle this responsibility and are permitted to sink to the level of puppets of Ottawa, then it will be the central government that will direct educational policy and administration in the provinces despite any facesaving formula that might be devised to give the illusion of continuing provincial autonomy. In existing circumstances only two or three of our ten provinces are in a position to carry this burden. The remainder are dependent on help from the federal government. Caught between the constitutional compulsion to provide adequate educational facilities and the staggering costs involved, many provinces are helpless to resist federal encroachment by means of conditional financial aid. It is often carefully hidden, but the federal initiative is a positive force in today's health, welfare and education programs.
This situation is directly contrary to the spirit of our constitution. There is little prospect of such provinces as Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Saskatchewan or Manitoba being regarded as independent and resolute regional units within the Canadian confederation when inadequate resources make them subservient to the central government. A healthy and workable confederation demands a constitution that will restore the ideal measure of regional autonomy envisaged in the British North America Act. It may well develop that the old regional groupings, are outdated. Some measure of regional consolidation may now be required. But this would, in no way, change the conditions and demands of confederation. If, for instance, a union of the maritime provinces takes place and the three prairie provinces amalgamate, this would not change the essential nature of the new union regional governments in relation to our constitution. We would then simply have one regional government for the Atlantic area instead of four and one for the prairies instead of three. The requirement for regional administrations to answer the needs of the people would remain the same as ever.
[Mr. Eitchie.l
I should like to mention what is common talk these days, the alienation of the west. Everyone assumes this is a new situation. But it has been around for a long time. It is not just related to lack of sales for wheat. It is a natural outgrowth of the long history of federal governments who have regarded western Canada as a mere appendage to central Canada. Only in the years 1958-62 did western Canada assume any real significance in the affairs of the nation. Since then, it has reverted to its role of exporting its natural resources to fuel the economic machine of central Canada. The present government, schizophrenic in its central theme that Canada extends only a stone's throw from Montreal, has immeasurably strengthened the very strong suspicion that western Canada will receive no support from central Canada. If the country has developed on an east-west axis, now so far as the west is concerned the flow is north-south. If Canada is to remain a confederation, then it must be recognized that it is a nation of regions. Otherwise, if nothing else, it may fracture off at the Lakehead. The federal government, with its preoccupation with its central Canada outlook, must revise its thrust if Canada is to remain a confederacy in the next 100 years.
There are many other arguments for entrenching the rights of the provinces under the confederation agreement. These, no doubt, will be brought out in detail in the discussions of the committee should it be established. But, as I suggested earlier, I believe first priority should be given to consideration of ways to curb the power of the executive by constitutional safeguards. If we do not do this, if we do not find means of restraining the small ruling clique, we may be sure they will never allow any meaningful amendment of the constitution with regard to provincial rights. I hope the committee will be established. I hope it will be based broadly enough to take in all shades of opinion, both within the recognized political parties and without. I hope, too, that discussion will not be confined to a narrow agenda drawn up by the government or that the committee itself will be emasculated by a government majority and government chairman whose thoughts and actions are dictated by the executive.

Mr. Speaker, I find that when elected to the House of Commons we all seem to become instant experts. I gather it is inherent in politics that we be all things to all men and there is a tremendous compulsion to display
January 27, 1970

full knowledge on any number of subjects in a very erudite fashion. I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will forgive me if, from time to time, in the course of my remarks, I indicate that I am somewhat unencumbered by a profound knowledge of constitutional politics, history and the law. But I do not apologize because in the last year and a half, and sometimes in this House, we have seen the political gods of this nation show an equal ignorance and lack of profundity. So, unimpeded by humility, I should like to reflect on two particular aspects of the resolution. The first is the method used to bring about constitutional change. Then, secondly, I should like to put forward some concept of what we might consider should be proposed in order to solve our chronic Canadian malady, the constitutional headache.
I think it is generally agreed that constitutional change is necessary. The constitution, being the root of all political and legal power, is the foundation upon which and within which our legal system operates. It must be flexible and at the same time unequivocal. The modern state, being complex, infringes tremendously at all levels of government on the rights of the individual. We must have a constitution which equally benefits and protects the citizen. The constitution adopted in 1867, as a result of judicial interpretation, the development of the double aspect theory, the water compartment theory and the restrictions on the peace, order and good government clause, is often interpreted by men out of the country with little knowledge of the nation or the nation's future. Coupled also with the evasion of the constitution by federal-provincial agreement, and a tactic of downright invasion by governments of other governmental spheres, we are left with a constitution which is at times almost impossible to decipher, which is obscure and which on many occasions cannot be determined.
Modern Canada is very different from Canada at the time the constitution was formed. In addition to that, I notice there are two distinct attitudes toward our constitution, largely dependent upon the region of the country from which one comes. Easterners generally consider the federal government to be the child of the provinces and therefore believe the provinces should be given appropriate powers. Westerners look at it in reverse. They consider their provinces to be children of the federal government and tend to accept more readily the centralization and consolidation of power in the federal authority.
Canadian Constitution
I believe the government is to be complimented for proposing the formation of this committee and also for giving the priority it has to constitutional change. Although it might be criticized in the sense that it will interfere in an immediate solution to some of our problems, I think in the long run it will certainly simplify and expedite answers to these problems. The method adopted is the federal-provincial conference. Any method has drawbacks and any method can be criticized.
It is difficult to constructively criticize a method and suggest good solid alternatives. But having adopted the method, I believe those who are engaged in the conference perhaps should accept a little constructive criticism, even though it comes from an hon. member who is not an expert on it. At the outset, it appears to me that some of the observations made in the House yesterday by members of the opposition are quite justified. I get the feeling that I, as an average taxpayer and citizen, am a bystander to a confrontation between big governments whereby the governments squabble over the power to tax, the power to control my destiny, the power to infringe upon my rights and all too often drift away from the concept that it is not what is best for the federal or provincial governments with which I am concerned but rather what is best for me as an average citizen. The suggestion that the provinces should have more taxing power, it seems to me, should have been coupled with the suggestion that there should be an over-all control over taxation at all levels of government before such a suggestion is put forward.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I say that no matter what office you might hold, the problems must be considered from the point of view of the individual citizen first and what he might need and want as a citizen of this country. It should not be a squabble between two governments trying to determine which politician shall have the most power. Politicians are always loth to surrender power once they get into office, and they have a tendency to want more and more of it, rationalizing their demands from time to time without approaching the matter in a rational and objective manner.
It is regrettable that no mechanism was set up in these conferences whereby individual citizens and groups could be heard. Constitutional change should not be the prerogative of politicians-I agree with some of the speakers

January 27. 1970
Canadian Constitution
who have expressed that view. Party dogma, party philosophy and the more or less temporal tenure of political office should not be factors that warp and distort the validity of the results of constitutional conferences. It is certainly pleasing to see that this committee will be empowered to call witnesses and hear the views of the Canadian public.
Another criticism that might well be put forward about the method that was adopted is that there is too much parochialism. Premier Bennett, the great ringmaster of the Social Credit circus in British Columbia, suggested at one conference that the northern boundary of British Columbia should be extended to include part of the Yukon, if not all of it. But if he had been looking at this matter from the point of view of the national interest, he could equally well have suggested that the southern boundary of the Yukon should be extended down into British Columbia and that a new province should be created. I must say I do not think that Premier Bennett is known for his concept of nationalism and for thinking in national terms, certainly not in British Columbia.
I think that there has been a rather blatant display by people who came to perform and not to confer; people who, mindful of the fact that they are wearing their television makeup and are on national television, sometimes drift a little away from the fact that they are there to consider what we want to have in a new constitution. I suggest that the conferences have been used for the blatant, chauvinistic purposes of political gain in the old home town. I refer here to the attack on the white paper. I do not know what that had to do with the constitution. It is certainly contemporary in the political sense, but it is not part of the constitutional conference.
I am gravely concerned about in camera sessions. I think that secrecy in government affairs is dangerous, and I suggest that the political climate greatly differs now from what it was at the time of the Quebec and Charlottetown conferences which were held in camera. Perhaps there was far greater reason for secrecy then that there is now. I am worried about the tremendous influence that can be brought to bear by bureaucrats at in camera meetings, and the great tendency of politicians to accept decisions made by bureaucrats as being very erudite and cogent. I think we should all warn the delegates to these conferences that this country is unlikely to accept a constitution that is a fait accompli by decisions made in camera.

I am rather disappointed that the terms of reference of this committee are confined to those declarations that have been made public. I look forward to seeing the person who is going to be able to confine that committee to its terms of reference. It will be a very interesting job indeed, but I do not think that the delegates will ever get away with presenting to the Canadian people a fait accompli constitution in the melee of a general election. The confrontation method leads to the intrusion of partisan politics in an approach to a new constitution. Provincial premiers, or perhaps even a prime minister, facing an election might take a rather different view if they did not have an election in the offing. For instance, the change in government in Manitoba brought about little change in attitude from the people in that province, and I do not think the people in that province really changed their minds so substantially about the constitution.
The criticisms I have made perhaps have more or less validity and cogency. I do not suggest that there is any adequate alternate way, but I am surprised that somebody has not given some consideration to the creation of a constitutional parliament, entirely objective in its deliberations, free of confrontation, independent of existing governments, representative of all regions, and empowered to listen to the people as well as to all levels of government.

Yes, and free of a few lawyers, too. This might not be a very valid alternative, but you have to admit it is a hell of a lot better than a revolution.
In dealing with these proposals for a new constitution, two matters of great importance should be noted: first, the entrenchment of civil rights in the constitution-I certainly welcome that suggestion-and second, the consideration of the division of powers, which are so essential in a federal state. I do not propose to dwell a great deal on the entrenchment of civil rights in the constitution. It is going to bring about a wholly new attitude toward legislation at all government levels, and certainly the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in the Drybones case, which was recently handed down, adds but a slight tremor to the earth shaking judicial decisions which will be handed down when civil rights are entrenched in the new constitution. It will be a money-maker for lawyers.

In dealing with the division between federal and provincial powers, we have to concede at the outset that the central or federal government should have the major instruments that are necessary to formulate the economic policy of the nation. The federal government must always be in a position to have its hands on the throttle of the economy of Canada. For instance, the attack on inflation should be primarily and exclusively something within the power of the federal government because it is a national problem.
Similarly, all problems that affect the national interest should rest with the federal government, and I would mention specifically foreign affairs. There should be adherence to the original concept that local governments should look after local and regional problems. The problem which arises, as I see it, is what happens when the local problems become so intense that they become of national concern-problems such as pollution, urban affairs, housing, consumer affairs, and standards of health. These things which were essentially local problems at one time have now become so national in their scope that they are considered to be problems of the whole of Canada.
For instance, according to the Hall report on medicare the reason the federal government entered the medicare field was, as the honourable judge suggested, that standards of health in Canada should be applied all across the country and therefore the federal government should act in this area. But the result has not been particularly satisfactory. It has not been what it would have been if the government had been able to act in a direct fashion without going into extensive consultations with the provinces. Sometimes such problems are very small in their subject matter and do not lend themselves to great, big, over-all reviews of the constitution. For instance, for years the Canadian Bar Association has been trying to set up a central registry for encumbrances and mortgages on aircraft but were continually met by the statement from the federal government that this would be unconstitutional.
In connection with all these problems, there must be a way in which the powers can be transferred from the provinces to the federal government and vice-versa, should the occasion in the contemporary scene demand it. Similarly, we are devoid of any throttle on the amount of taxation that can be imposed. The provincial governments have unlimited taxation powers in their own field, and so
Canadian Constitution
does the federal government. The result is that nobody can say, "wait, there is too much taxation now". There is no way in which that can be controlled.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The question is how can these problems be solved? My suggestion is that we give some consideration to that venerable company of old Canadians who share this building with us, and who respond so quaintly, so quickly and in such numbers to the tinkle of their little bell. I have never argued that the Senate should continue to exist in its present form. I think it could be reformed and changed into a very viable body. This baby-blanket of Parliament Hill could be of tremendous use by becoming the arbiter between the provincial and the federal governments of this country.
I think we should propose to the Canadian people that the Senate take on new functions. I suggest, first, that it should be appointed by a constitutionally entrenched formula, getting representatives from the provinces and the federal government, and that its objectivity, its independence from both governments should be entrenched in that formula so that it cannot be manipulated by either the federal or the provincial governments.
Secondly, it should have no legislative powers at all in the direct sense.
Thirdly, it should be empowered to determine when a transfer of legislative power should take place from the provinces to the federal government, or vice versa, depending upon the applications made to it by either of these levels of government. It should have the staff and the structure to investigate where the national or provincial interests might lie, in a broad sense, throughout the nation. For example, the pollution problem could be put before such a Senate, and it could decide which government and to what extent which government should be responsible for it. It could say that the federal government should take the responsibility entirely, or that the federal government should take certain aspects of it and certain other aspects should be left to the provinces.
Fourthly, it could be used to control the over-all imposition of taxation. For example, it could advise a government when it was imposing a new tax that it had gone too far in certain regions of the country because the provinces concerned had already taxed those regions to a certain level. That would be a

powerful political factor in preventing the imposition of too much taxation.
Fifthly, it could serve as a fact-finding body for the federal and provincial governments, and thus abolish the necessity for royal commissions. It could even inquire as to what has happened to the Royal Commission on the Status of Women.
Sixthly, it could be the arbiter of intra-provincial disputes, and seventhly, it could serve as a national law reform commission and concern itself with the uniformity of laws throughout the country.
Eighthly, it could have a judicial arm to solve disputes arising out of constitutional matters. I would not suggest that the Senators all be selected for the same purpose. You might have a general body of Senators selected, and then have some selected because of their specific knowledge to serve for a certain purpose or for a certain term of years.
I have just about exhausted my time, Mr. Speaker. Whatever happens to this committee that we are now forming, I think we all look forward to watching its progress in helping to shape a new constitution. Above all, I hope that when it finally reports to this House it will have more luck than the Standing Committee on Northern Affairs did.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) for his courtesy.

I should like to give a very warm welcome to this motion, Mr. Speaker. For many years I have been convinced that the elected members of Parliament, representing as they do every region in Canada and many different groups and interests, are pre-eminently suited to deal with the future framework of the Canadian political system, and that, after all, is what the constitution is.
I am personally interested because I pressed this idea of a parliamentary committee on the constitution in correspondence and in conference on the former prime minister, Mr. Pearson. He always agreed with me, but it was never the appropriate time to do anything about it. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) may remember that I urged support for this idea upon him a few weeks after he became a member of this House. Yesterday, he introduced the motion to set up such a

committee, and it would be most ungracious of me not to acknowledge that fact with gratitude.
For myself, I am profoundly convinced that the committee can play a vital role in the constitutional development necessary to the future needs of Canada. Whatever the utility and necessity of continuing committees of civil servants and other experts, whatever the role of federal-provincial constitutional conferences, I am confident that in the ultimate analysis this Parliament is and should remain the major guardian of a strong but flexible federal system.
I do not share the attitude of those who regard the process of constitutional revision with impatience and who call for action on economic bread-and-butter issues. There is a false division here. Modern governments, of necessity, deal with economic issues. They must be concerned with full employment, housing, health, pollution, urban problems and even recreational facilities. They are called upon to improve the quality of life as well as to maintain economic growth. But governments either perform these functions, or fail to perform them because of the constitutional compact within which they must all work.
In a country with regions widely separated from each other by language and cultural divisions, as well as by distance and different economic conditions, as in Canada, agreement as to the constitutional structure is essential. Constitutional improvement and clarification are required for the smooth functioning of our system of government; indeed, for its existence. Constitutional revision, therefore, is of great practical importance and not an exercise to be reserved for constitutional lawyers and experts, but the very stuff of politics and the concern of all elected members.
I can sympathize with provincial premiers who speak out about the ancient and modern problems, such as freight rates and regional inequalities. I am sure much can be done within the existing constitution and by an intensified process of co-operative federalism to deal with some of these problems, but this does not absolve us from considering the constitutional framework of our whole constitutional system.
I am not one of those who think that the revision of the British North America Act is unimportant. The Prime Minister, in his speech, referred to cliches about the constitution. Perhaps I shall be guilty of some of the cliches to which he referred. But however
January 27, 1970

obvious some of these remarks may be they need to be repeated from time to time.
The British North America Act is a colonial statute, passed by the British parliament in Westminster more than a hundred years ago. It is obsolete in form and uninspiring in style. It deals with the needs of small and mainly agricultural societies. Today, we are called upon to deal with vast urban conglomerations. It would be miraculous if the dispositions of a hundred years ago did not require review.
I am personally not iconoclastic about some of the basic provisions of the British North America Act. Some of those provisions, namely, those dealing with division of powers between the federal and provincial legislatures, may remain basically sound and require little change. It is to me, however, quite unthinkable that with the development of new problems of housing, pollution and renewal it does not require a new look.
The federal Parliament, as we all know, has employed the spending power to intervene from time to time in fields regarded as exclusively provincial. This has been bitterly resented by some provinces, notably the province of Quebec. Such a use of the spending power is nowhere explicit in the British North America Act. The limits of consequences of the exercise of the spending power need to be spelled out in the new constitution.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
There remains in our constitutional set-up one crucial problem that must be resolved if Canada is to continue to be united. Federations, if they are healthy, are based on the consent of all regions, but there is in Canada a bone of contention which threatens to destroy consent. I refer to the difference of opinion about the degree of centralization in respect of legislation on social issues which is acceptable to different parts of Canada.
The Prime Minister of Quebec, at the last federal-provincial constitutional conference, made it quite clear that whatever other provinces might do, Quebec was not prepared to see the federal government interfere by use of the spending power, shared-cost programs or any other device, in fields such as social services and housing; such centralization would be resisted. In saying this he was repeating what had been said by his predecessors of all parties. I do not doubt that he speaks for Quebec in this regard, but I believe that the other provinces are willing, and in some cases anxious, for federal inter-
Canadian Constitution
vention in these fields. They do not wish to be hampered in securing national action on some of these matters because of Quebec's reluctance.
It was for this reason, Mr. Speaker, that some of us used the phrase "special status for Quebec". Perhaps it was an unfortunate phrase. It seemed to some to smack of condescension and concession. I emphasize, nevertheless, that the basic problem which remains is: How are we to organize our constitution so that Quebec can retain autonomy in fields in which her special culture demands it, without forcing upon the other provinces a decentralization which seems to some of them excessive?
I believe this is the crux of our constitutional problem, and I think that perhaps M. Bertrand was on the right track when he suggested that the device of delegation might be used by other provinces desiring it. It would have to be a refined process of delegation and be terminable only after an agreed period. The British North America Act says nothing about delegation. I believe the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council-perhaps the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) will correct me if I am wrong-has said that there is no power of legislative delegation within our present constitutional system.
I suggest that the committee ought to explore this avenue, because I believe that by following-up the matter of delegation and by studying the implications of some sort of permanency of delegation, we might find the answer to what I call the dilemma of our constitution.
There are three more subjects upon which I wish to touch lightly, Mr. Speaker. The first is the charter of human rights or a constitutional bill of rights. I hope that this Parliament and government will not flag in their determination to bring such charter into existence. There has developed an academic school of thought which downgrades the importance of such charter or constitutional bill of rights. I am afraid that some members of our provincial governments have paid undue attention to this school of thought. These people claim that to enshrine basic fundamental freedoms in a constitution is (a) to limit them, and (b) to hand over the protection of these fundamental political rights to the tender mercies of judicial review rather than to the protection of politically-elected governments and Parliaments.
I think neither of these objections is valid. Such declarations in our fundamental consti-

January 27, 1970
Canadian Constitution
tutional law have an immense educational value. They clarify for all the human and individual basic rights in a free democracy and, in addition, they provide useful and needed instruments to strike down the overzealous exercise of legislative interference with fundamental rights of the citizen. I know this statement to be valid because of my career at the Bar. I suggest that nobody familiar with history will say that leaders of nations do not from time to time attempt to interfere, sometimes with the best intentions in mind, with those fundamental rights which we all should have.
I should now like to say a word about the amending formula which is essential to any successful rewriting of the constitution. This party has opposed, and I hope will continue to oppose, any rigid system which would give to an individual province the power of veto, no matter how small, in the field of constitutional revision. We successfully opposed, and continue to oppose, the unlamented Fulton-Fa-vreau formula. We think that certain provisions of a fundamental nature could be enshrined in the constitution in such a way that the unanimous consent of the federal and provincial legislatures would be required for any change.
Examples of what I mean might be found in a charter of human rights, language rights and the right to free and regular elections. For instance, the constitution might contain various provisions which could not be changed without unanimous consent, whereas economic matters could be amended by a more simple and less rigid formula.
Perhaps the most recent federal-provincial constitutional conference was very close to the mark when it suggested that three out of four senatorial districts or three out of five such regions, including British Columbia- this was a suggestion of the Premier of British Columbia-might provide a consensus justifying federal interference in the provincial realm of shared-cost programs. 1 suggest to the House that a formula similar to that suggested to be applied to shared-cost programs might be applied to the amending of the constitution. Something of this sort is essential.

In general, I welcome the assertion that the federal government has a wide range of power to act in order to alleviate the unhappy situation of individuals and provinces through the constitutional spending power. Since the Second World War, use of the practically unrestricted federal spending power has enabled Canadian governments to do as much as has been done to create more equal opportunities in the less favoured regions of the country. We must recognize, however, that the federal spending power has been abused at times and that extreme care must be used in the future. It may now be desirable, in fact, to spell out the provision that the federal spending power should not be used as a means of getting around any agreed constitutional division of powers.
The document tries to make a distinction between what are called income security programs, income insurance and social services. The distinction is very unclear and fuzzy. The definitions used are often circuitous. I find it difficult to say whether I agree that social services should be exclusively provincial, because it is almost impossible to tell what the federal government means by this section of the proposal. I gather it would be left entirely to the courts to decide whether a program was mainly one of income security and therefore under federal jurisdiction, or whether it was mainly one of social services and therefore under provincial jurisdiction.
There is no question that the distribution of jurisdiction relating to social services and social welfare is considered to be very important by some provinces. That being so, it is very important that we are clear on how the powers are divided, if they are to be divided. I think it most unsatisfactory to propose leaving this distinction to the courts. The problem is really one of policy, not one of law, and legal solutions such as the courts provide are of use primarily in solving legal problems. What we need in this regard is a clear distinction and definition in terms of policy.
The federal government in its document also asserts its jurisdiction to handle special cases such as involving Indians and veterans. In general, this responsibility must continue. But we must be careful that we do not get into another constitutional strait jacket. One wonders, for example, about the possibility of making Indians full provincial citizens and integrating them into the provincial political
January 27, 1970

Canadian Constitution
system. There might be similar problems with respect to the handling of immigrants.
What is most important is constitutional flexibility-a fairly clear delineation in terms of policy as to what powers should belong to whom, and who is responsible for doing what, while at the same time maintaining freedom of manoeuvre. The federal proposals do not seem to take into account the evidence that a number of provincial governments are concerned about Indians, are concerned about immigrants, and some are even concerned about veterans, strange as those ideas might appear to the federal government. Do I understand from the federal proposals that the federal government proposes to take no account whatever of these provincial interests?
The federal proposals do envision one substantial change in the present distribution of power. Unfortunately, the proposal is highly controversial and seems designed only to provoke the province of Quebec and hostility from other provinces, to no apparent good end. I refer to the proposal to change the 1951 amendment to the British North America Act, the one which made pensions a matter of joint jurisdiction and gave the provinces priority. The federal government which brought about 1951 amendment now proposes to change the priority from provincial to federal. Why, one is not told; and what would be accomplished thereby is not at all clear.
There is no point in changing this part of the British North America Act unless a change in the program itself is contemplated. There are essentially two programs, and only two: one is the Quebec Pension Plan and the other is the Canada Pension Plan. Both seem to be working very well and the provincial governments in particular are pleased with the funds which are made available to them through the Canada Pension Plan.
There would seem to be only two possible reasons for wishing such a change. The federal government should tell us now which of the two reasons it is. The first is the possibility that the federal government wishes to eliminate the Quebec Pension Plan and to integrate the people in the province of Quebec into the same kind of pension program which exists in the rest of Canada. The second possibility is that the federal government wants to change the Canada Pension Plan to a kind of gigantic money-grab. It may wish to see the funds which the provincial governments now have for their own capital
development transferred to the federal treasury, so it can squander at will as it has been so used to doing. There may be a third reason, but it is not at all clear what that might be and it is incumbent on this government to tell the country what it has in mind and why it is making this particular proposal. If I may sum up this point, the working paper is probably best interpreted as a direct rebuff to the proposals of the province of Quebec.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
There is nothing wrong with the federal government stating where it stands in relation to other proposals, but it should never do so in the deliberately provocative way that it has. Its use of the word "tentative" to describe what has been the explicit and detailed policy of the government of Quebec during the past six or seven years indicates a general attitude which I think is highly undesirable. This is simply confrontation politics and contributes in no way at all to Canadian unity. The degree of inflexibility indicated in the federal working paper on social services and income security is in no way desirable. It is a symptom, I should say, of the autocracy and rigidity which marks the policy of the present federal administration.

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been able to attend the House during most of this debate. If I may say with respect to the House, and I feel sure hon. members will generally agree, it has been a first-class debate. I have enjoyed it thoroughly. I think it has in some way highlighted for the people of Canada the importance of this exercise in constitutional review and its importance for the future of our country.
I know there have been critics of the way the constitutional review has been conducted. Criticisms have been expressed both in the country at large and, indeed, during the course of this debate. We have heard it said that the entire process of constitutional review is irrelevant to the main issues and questions that are before the country, and that the government in proceeding to a deliberate review of the constitution and the British North America Act is not dealing with what have been called the gut issues facing Canada. I think Premier Thatcher put it in the strongest possible terms when he said that the province of Saskatchewan may have had 100 problems facing the future of the people of Saskatchewan, but the constitution was the 101st. In any event, that has been said.

January 27, 1970
Canadian Constitution
The critics have maintained that the government should be dealing with the main issues of the day and should be concentrating its attention on efforts of reform in respect of the issues of cities such as traffic, transportation, urban renewal, housing and pollution; that it should be directing its efforts toward overcoming the poisoning of our environment on land, in the waters and in the air; that it should be concentrating on developing a national resources policy and on taking an inventory of those resources and assuring the production and manufacturing of these resources in Canada under Canadian control. These critics have said we should be dealing with issues that are economic, particularly those now affecting the country

inflation, the cost of living, prices, rents and wages.
I think the first answer to all this criticism is that we categorically deny that we have not been dealing with these issues. Indeed, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said, no program of any advantage to the people of Canada has in any way been delayed or postponed by reason of this constitutional review.
I think the more fundamental answer is perhaps to recognize that there are many people in Canada, and might I say many people in this House of Commons, who fail to appreciate the relevance of the constitution, as a fundamental document under which we conduct our affairs in a federal state, to the problems of our everyday life. They fail to recognize that the British North America Act is a fundamental and primary document affecting the relationship between federal and provincial governments. By the very process of reviewing that document we are dealing with the gut issues facing Canada; we are dealing with the bread and butter issues of this nation. A federal state by its very nature involves limitation on the powers and authority of the federal government, and corresponding limitations on the authority of provincial governments. These limitations of powers are set forth primarily in articles 91 and 92 of the British North America Act. This distribution of powers was agreed to over 100 years ago.
There are those who maintain that the constitution was largely rewritten by decisions of the Privy Council, particularly under the auspices of Lord Watson and Lord Haldane over the years, and that the document as currently interpreted by the courts does not resemble what the Fathers of Confederation intended to say and have written down.

New economic realities permit many people to question the current application of that distribution of powers as set forth in the BNA Act. Regarding the concentration in urban centres, the Economic Council of Canada suggests that by 1980 over 80 per cent of us will be living in large metropolitan areas in this country. Regional disparity is growing and the gaps are growing wider. This was eloquently put by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis)-this has happened since the French-speaking Canadians have a new awareness of their own cultural identity particularly in Quebec.
For what it is worth, my own view is that in the past generation the federal government has failed to exercise fully its available constitutional powers, the powers available to the federal government under the present constitution of Canada. For what it is worth, I feel that the federal government over the past generation has failed to test its constitutional muscle before the courts of this country, when such testing was necessary. I believe the federal government has been constitutionally timid. Perhaps it has been traumatized by past decisions of the Privy Council.
Certainly I would think, and submit to the House and Your Honour, that we as a federal government and as a Parliament of the people of Canada, have been insufficiently resourceful in testing the trade and commerce clause, the residual clause of peace, order and good government, and in confining property and civil rights to its proper ambit. We have placed overreliance on the criminal power, particularly as it has been used to regulate economic affairs. I refer particularly to the Combines Investigation Act which is really economic regulation and control by criminal power. This involves a stiffer burden of proof than the state can discharge in many cases. This has resulted in the merger clauses becoming ineffective. It prevents the ordinary citizen from obtaining civil damages from those who monopolize and conspire to fix prices. It also prevents cease and desist orders and injunctions to prevent action in respect of which a remedy is sought.
Notwithstanding my view that we have been constitutionally timid, I think the critics fail to realize or admit that the ultimate longterm solution to the economic and environmental issues in Canada-those issues which will demand our attention in the 1970s- involve a review of the fundamental constitutional framework under which the country operates.
January 27, 1970

I suggest that the federal government ought to explore exclusive jurisdiction or at least joint jurisdiction over these areas. The point was well taken by the hon. member for Gren-ville-Carleton (Mr. Blair). The federal government should explore this jurisdiction in respect of matters or urban renewal and other urban issues, the environment, resources, development, inflation, consumer credit, and so on.
It is true that the Prime Minister and this government have recognized this. On the other hand, there may be other powers now found in article 91 that might now be more conveniently exercised and more efficiently exercised by the provinces. I think we should envisage more flexibility in joint jurisdiction and in the transferring and delegation of powers from one jurisdiction to another under proper circumstances.
The Leader of the Opposition accused the Prime Minister of playing confrontation politics with Quebec. I am not going to get involved in an argument at this stage, but I suggest to him that a federal state by its very nature involves confrontation at times between the federal and provincial jurisdictions. There is always a flowing and ebbing of power to and fro in these jurisdictions. This is particularly true between Ottawa and Quebec.

The province of Quebec objects to certain centralizing influences which can be acceptable to other provinces. Why? Because the province of Quebec is the home of a people, because the French Canadian people has its own traditions, its own language, its own law.
If I were a French Canadian, living in the province of Quebec, I would insist on two things. First, I would insist on the need for a heavy representation in the House and in the federal cabinet. I would insist also to see the French Canadians adequately represented in Ottawa, and it seems obvious to me that they are not too badly represented in this government, for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is one of them.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In fact, French Canadians have been appointed Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, Minister of National Defence, Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, Secretary of State. There are also other ministers of great talent who
Canadian Constitution
represent here the French Canadian fact in North America.
Then, if I were a French Canadian living in Quebec, I would insist on the principle that Quebec must be strong, have enough resources to fulfil its responsibilities under the constitution, and enjoy enough constitutional powers to mobilize the forces of its identity, something which invariably leads to a conflict of interests between the federal and the provincial governments.
It is necessary that there be confrontation from time to time in order to clarify the terms for the Canadian public.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)

I should like to say a few words about the current status of the negotiations at the federal-provincial conferences. It seems to me we have not yet had a joinder of issue. The federal positions have been set forth on a number of major items. They have been published and hon. members are aware of the publication. Therefore, it is not necessary for me to recite them. Except for the province of Quebec, the province of New Brunswick and in respect of certain issues the province of Manitoba, the provinces have been reluctant to reveal their own hands. There has been a failure to come to grips or, as lawyers would say, to join issue with the federal government so that true discussion can be possible.
It has also been suggested that negotiation in respect of a constitution under the lights of television may not be too productive because this may not be the best possible atmosphere. For my own part, I believe in an open democracy. So far as television is concerned, I believe it is inevitable that television will be brought into the proceedings of committees and into this chamber so that the ordinary person in Canada will be placed in the position of people in the galleries. If this means the rules will have to be revised to accommodate this place to the instrument of instant communication, then the rules will have to be revised. At any rate, at the federal-provincial conferences we will now have working sessions, an euphemism for closed sessions.
A new or revised constitution is not easily packaged. There is no instant solution. I say to the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. Flemming) that there is no reason the British North America Act cannot be the base from which we operate. There will be some hard negotiation, not only between govern-

January 27, 1970
Canadian Constitution
ments but between regions and the people living in these regions.
The Prime Minister and this government have opened a total review of the constitution. There will be give and take concerning what we believe the people of Canada as a whole should have in terms of legislative authority, and what the people of individual regions and provinces should have. There will be hard bargaining. I want to suggest to the hon. member for York South, who made his usual able contribution to this debate, that perhaps he is using sophistry when he suggested the conferences so far have been merely exercises in auctioneering whereby the provincial and federal governments auction power at the expense of the Canadian people.
A new constitution or any amendment to a constitution implies some bargaining. We will concede to the hon. member and to the House that the negotiations cannot be solely between governments but must be between the provinces and the people of Canada who form this great country. The people of Canada must be involved. If they are to be involved, then we as a Parliament must be involved. We are the forum of the nation. We are still the theatre of this great country.

I do not intend to recapitulate all the arguments that have been advanced during the debate on the resolution before the House. No doubt, such a committee can very efficiently contribute to the examination in depth of the constitution presently in force.
However, the measure of this contribution will be, to a certain extent, determined by the way in which the committee's work will be co-ordinated with that of the federal and provincial governments. We also hope that the constitutional review will be strengthened by the combined voices of senators and members of Parliament.

For this reason, we see this committee as one having a positive and influential role if its work is to be related to the constitutional review process. The federal government and the provinces in their constitutional negotiations have, perforce, had to establish a plan, a methodology, for review. This has involved selecting certain areas for priority study, if only for the purpose of defining the issues. To the extent that there is a limitation proposed in the ambit of the study of the committee, it is the same limitation to which the federal

government and the provinces will have to submit themselves in relation to the process of total review of the constitution. The discipline of some defined approach to constitutional review is implicit by the very nature of the enterprise, and that same discipline is all that is sought to he imposed on the committee.
It may well be asked: What is this process? I believe the Prime Minister has already outlined the background of our involvement in constitutional review and how the process went from a review of individual rights and the institutions of the federal government into a review of the division of powers. But the point he made with great force was that the total review of the constitution implies an organized review, a controlled review and a controlled development of our constitution. The federal government, as I have said, has sought to move from the rights of citizens and institutions of our federation into a study of the more contentious subjects involved in the division of powers. For this reason we have been concerned with questions relating to a charter of rights and the judiciary, two matters with which I have had a particular concern as chairman at the ministerial level.
The government hoped to place to the forefront, in a constitutional review, the reassessment of the protection of the rights of individuals in our society. We hope there will be an increased recognition of what we consider to be the necessity of formal recognition of certain basic rights of Canadians. We believe this should be implicit in the constitution of Canada. In fact, it seems to me it would be really inconceivable in respect of the establishment of a new constitutional framework for Canada if the principle of freedom of assembly, freedom of religion and freedom of speech were not enshrined as part of the constitution of this country.

freedom from discrimination.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If I can
summarize the reasons for the establishment of the committee, I would say first that governments cannot operate in a vacuum. They need a responsive climate of public opinion. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) said rulers cannot decide the rules under which we are to be ruled. I agree. However, I think he would concede that governments have to lead and take responsibility. I believe this government has taken its responsibility and has declared itself by way of its proposi-
January 27, 1970

Canadian Constitution
tions before the country. We have put ourselves on the line. The federal government has now declared its position on a number of items. Parliament should now review, test and probe those positions. As the Prime Minister said in his opening speech in introducing the resolution, Parliament should nurture the necessary consensus for nationhood. Constitutions in the past have been written only under the fire of crisis. A sense of urgency has had to dominate the minds of men before constitutions could be written or rewritten- revolution, anarchy, secession.
Our controlled procedure of rational discussion, discussion of the issues in the widest possible national form, is the first time in history that a nation has tried to anticipate and head-off a crisis, and to dissolve it before it crystallized, by rational discussion among free men.

Perhaps I could come back to the theme so eloquently developed during the debate by the member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau), a name which has a particular signification for all Canadians of good will. Indeed, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe who sat in the House for a long time and who for many years, headed the department I am honored of now being in charge of personified the open-mindedness that has always characterized French-speaking members and the whole French-speaking population.
This spirit springs from the desire of making our federal system work, of helping to build a strong and united Canada which, at the same time, makes room for linguistic, cultural and geographical variety. This is not to say that differences do not exist, but that we have the experience of different views, of a possible synthesis, of the acceptation of better solutions that are possible but not perfect.
We, the English-speaking Canadians have, in a certain way, lived under federalism, like the French-speaking Canadians for more than a 100 years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I sincerely thank my colleagues, Mr. Speaker.
Our experience is made up of pragmatism and generosity from both parts.
I am sure that the representatives of all political parties who took part in this debate are faithful to the same traditions.
But I must add that, for its part, the federal government will never give up its place as a front-line defender of National unity and efficient federalism. For that reason, we have been most diligent in the realization of our linguistic objectives as required by the Official Languages Act which, was drawn up in the light of public opinion.
In the constitutional field, we do not submit to this House any fixed and unchanging positions.
We merely suggest, a means of taking part in this review of the constitution, that is the creation of a parliamentary committee. This will allow for a greater political involvement in this process, as was pointed out by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Roberts) whose very wise words should be kept in mind by those who are interested in this question of constitutional review.
We ask the House to vote in favour of the motion. We believe that a parliamentary committee would make a great contribution to the long and detailed study which is at the very basis of any constitutional review.

Mr. Speaker, writing a new constitution or reworking the present one will demand reservoirs of good will, understanding and tolerance in Canada. This good will cannot be imposed upon the Canadian people by experts, bureaucrats or mandarins. Essentially, this process is a political one, reconciling the legitimate interests and approaches of various parts of Canada. It is a political one, but it need not be a partisan process. The issues are for the people to decide, not for experts to proclaim. This committee, if it meets the hopes of the government, and indeed the hopes of the House, will bring the constitution home to the people of Canada.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have made shorter speeches than the one I shall have to make tonight, but not many. Like the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) I should like to make the comment that this has been an excellent debate during which valuable contributions have been made from all quarters of the House, and indeed I should like to add to those who were commended by the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Justice himself with respect to the very useful contribution he made to this debate just now.

January 27, 1970
Canadian Constitution
We all agree that the task oi reviewing and rewriting our constitution is a difficult one. It seems to take a long time. There are many occasions when we feel frustrated, when there is the temptation to feel that it is hopeless. But because of the importance of a basic constitution to a country like ours, we must press forward, and I think it can be said that the Members of Parliament from all parts of Canada have made it clear during the course of this debate that that is what we shall do. I trust the result will be an excellent piece of work by this committee which will press forward the cause that is now in hand.
In the minute or two that are left there are one or two things I would like to say. In a sense, the Minister of Justice gave me a text to use for what I wanted to say when he asserted that at times the federal government has been too timid in testing its federal authority. Whether he noted it or not, I was applauding that statement and I welcome it. It does seem to me that one of the dangers, because of the time it is taking to review and rewrite our constitution, is for certain things that could now be done to be left undone or to be allowed to wait.
I was not impressed by the assertion of the Minister of Justice that nothing has been delayed because of this discussion. After all, that is an argument by assertion and the minister and I are both good at it. But the fact of the matter is that the minister was right when he said that this government has not tested the authority that it now has, and I name in particular such fields as housing, pollution and income security.
I quite disagree with the interpretation of the working paper on income security and social services that was offered tonight by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). I would say that whatever may be the outcome, there are areas of federal authority asserted in that document that no one will challenge, and the government should act on them now in terms of such programs as the guaranteed annual income and other ways of supporting the incomes of all the Canadian people.
As I said, in all these fields that I have indicated, such as housing, pollution and income security, and in the other fields that the Minister of Justice himself cited tonight, I do not think that the federal Parliament or the federal government have yet tested their authority to the extent that they might have done. I hope that concurrent with the attempt to rewrite our basic document and come up with a constitution that will stand us for many decades to come, this Parliament will insist on the government proceeding with policies and programs for which it now has authority and which this country and our people sorely need.
